sections.h2: Loveland roofs, block by block
sections.html:
Loveland sits at 4,997 feet in Larimer County, where the Big Thompson River leaves the canyon and the foothills give way to the plains. That position shapes every roof in town. Downslope winds come off the hogbacks on the west side, hail cells build over the foothills and drop on the city in the afternoon, and the sun at this elevation ages asphalt faster than it does at sea level.

The housing stock is layered. Downtown, between the Sweetheart City core and Lake Loveland, the bungalows, foursquares, and brick cottages from the 1900s through the 1930s carry steep pitches, original plank decking, and often two or three generations of shingles. The ranches and split-levels between Taft Avenue and Garfield Avenue date to the 1950s through the 1970s, with lower pitches, long eaves, and attic ventilation that was never adequate. West of Wilson Avenue and south of Highway 402, the subdivisions built from the 1990s through the 2010s, Mariana Butte, Seven Lakes, Alford Meadows, Hunters Run, and Thompson Valley, carry builder-grade architectural shingles that are now reaching the end of their service life all at once. Around Boyd Lake and Centerra the roofs are newer still, and the HOA rulebooks are thicker.

What we see on inspection: layered shingles over plank decks downtown, ice dams on the mid-century north eaves, and wind-lifted shingles and delayed granule loss in the subdivisions.

sections.h2: Hail and wind history in Loveland
sections.html:
Loveland is squarely inside the Front Range hail corridor. The reports the National Weather Service has logged for the city include 1.75 inch hail on July 13, 2011, golf ball hail across Loveland, Fort Collins, and Timnath on June 12, 2017, 1.25 to 1.75 inch hail on the evening of July 5, 2019, and a 1.75 inch report at Lake Loveland Park on August 5, 2023. Many of those storms tracked straight down the Highway 34 corridor.

Wind is the other half of the story. On the night of January 6 into January 7, 2020, a weather station just north of Carter Lake recorded a 100 mile per hour gust, the strongest of that event anywhere in the state, and that is the same airflow that strips ridge caps on west Loveland and along the Big Thompson every winter. Chinook events like that one are why we nail six per shingle and seal every ridge, even when a lesser pattern would pass code.

sections.h2: Roof systems that hold up here
sections.html:
For most Loveland homes the right answer is a Class 4 impact-resistant architectural shingle over full ice barrier and synthetic underlayment with a high-wind nailing pattern. It satisfies the city code and earns the premium credit many carriers offer. Read our guide to Class 4 shingles and Colorado insurance discounts before you pick a product.

On the west side and on the custom homes above Mariana Butte we install more standing seam metal, because it shrugs off both hail and 100 mile per hour wind. Downtown, where a bungalow needs to keep its character, synthetic slate and shake gives the historic profile with a Class 4 rating. For the 1950s ranches with low pitch sections we often pair shingles on the main roof with a membrane over the low-slope porch or addition rather than forcing shingles where they will fail.

sections.h2: Permits, inspections, and HOA approvals in Loveland
sections.html:
Roof replacement in the city is permitted through the City of Loveland Building Division at 410 East 5th Street. The division's roofing policy, in effect since June 1, 2022, sets three thresholds: repairs up to one square (100 square feet) need no permit; anything over one square and up to 49 percent of the roof needs a like-for-like permit; anything over 49 percent requires a full tear-off to the deck and a permit. Replacing 50 percent or more of an asphalt roof requires Class 4 shingles tested to UL 2218. Ice barrier must run from the eave to at least 24 inches past the interior face of the exterior wall, 36 inches on roofs 8:12 or steeper, and drip edge is required at eaves and rakes. The job closes with a final inspection, and we hand you the approved record with your closeout photos.

Addresses outside city limits, including Masonville, Campion, Carter Lake, and the acreages along County Road 18, fall under Larimer County, which requires a Class A covering countywide, Class 4 asphalt shingles on replacements, the same ice barrier, and a signed roofing certification. We confirm jurisdiction from the address before we quote.

HOA review is routine in Mariana Butte, Seven Lakes, Boyd Lake, and most of the Centerra neighborhoods. Expect a color and profile approval, and in some communities a minimum of Class 4. Colorado law also prevents an HOA from blocking a homeowner who wants to replace a wood shake roof with a less flammable material. We prepare the submittal with product sheets and a color sample so the board can approve it at the next meeting.

sections.h2: Hail season and insurance claims
sections.html: Hail season on the northern Front Range runs May through August, with June the busiest month. The storm chasers arrive within 48 hours. Our advice is to get a photo-documented inspection first, then decide whether to open a claim. If you do file, our insurance claim roofing process covers the adjuster meeting and the scope review once you have signed with us. We never pay or waive deductibles; Colorado law (C.R.S. 6-22-105) prohibits it, and the roofer who offers to is telling you who they are. Here is what to do in the first week after a hail storm.

sections.h2: A Loveland roofer, not a Loveland mailing address
sections.html: Every roof replacement and every hail repair we do in Loveland is within ten minutes of our shop. That means a crew on your roof the morning after a storm, a project lead who can stop by when the adjuster shows up, and a phone number that will still ring in five years when you have a warranty question. Call (970) 430-5884 or book a free inspection and we will walk the roof, photograph it, and give you a written itemized estimate.

faq.q: How much is a roofing permit in Loveland?
faq.a: The City of Loveland Building Division sets permit fees on a valuation schedule, so the fee rises with the size and cost of the roof. We include the permit fee as its own line in the written estimate so you can see it, and we pull the permit and schedule the final inspection as part of the job. Call the division at (970) 962-2505 if you want to verify a fee before you sign.

faq.q: Does Loveland require Class 4 shingles?
faq.a: Yes, when 50 percent or more of an asphalt roof is replaced. The city roofing policy in effect since June 2022 requires UL 2218 Class 4 impact-resistant shingles on those jobs, with full tear-off to the deck. Partial repairs of 49 percent or less may match the existing shingle. Most Loveland HOAs follow the city rule, and many insurers give a premium credit for Class 4.

faq.q: When is hail season in Loveland?
faq.a: May through August, with June historically the most active month. Documented Loveland storms include July 2011, June 2017, July 2019, and August 2023. The pattern is late afternoon cells that build over the foothills and move east down the Highway 34 corridor, so west and central Loveland often take the first hit.

faq.q: Do you work on unincorporated Larimer County addresses around Loveland?
faq.a: Yes. Masonville, Campion, Carter Lake, and the county road acreages around the city are all in our daily range. Those addresses are permitted through Larimer County rather than the city, which requires a Class A covering, Class 4 asphalt shingles on replacement roofs, ice barrier, and a roofing certification form. We confirm the jurisdiction before quoting and handle the paperwork.

sections.h2: Why Fort Collins mandated Class 4 shingles
sections.html:
The rule came out of the storms. On June 24, 2014, hail up to 2.5 inches fell on east Fort Collins and Timnath, tearing roofing and siding off homes in Harmony Park and punching holes in a grocery store roof nearby. On June 12, 2017, golf ball hail hit the east side again while 2.75 inch stones fell on Severance. On June 19, 2018, golf ball hail was reported in Fort Collins, LaPorte, and Wellington in the same evening. The city responded: for permits applied for after January 12, 2019, every asphalt shingle roof in Fort Collins must be UL 2218 Class 4 impact resistant.

The storms did not stop. On July 27, 2022, tennis ball to baseball hail fell on the Timnath side of the city line, and the summers of 2023 and 2025 brought repeated 1 to 1.25 inch reports across the south and east sides. At 5,003 feet in Larimer County, Fort Collins sits where foothill-born cells reach the plains with their energy intact. Hail season runs May through August. Here is how to tell if your Fort Collins roof has hail damage, because on a Class 4 shingle the bruising looks different.

sections.h2: What we see on Fort Collins roofs
sections.html:
Old Town and the historic neighborhoods on both sides of College Avenue carry the oldest roofs in the region: 1880s to 1920s foursquares and bungalows with 10:12 and steeper pitches, skip-sheathed or plank decks, box gutters, and chimneys that were never flashed properly the first time. Several blocks are designated historic districts or landmarks, which adds a review step. Campus West and the neighborhoods around CSU are 1950s to 1970s ranches and rentals, low pitch, long eaves, chronically under-ventilated, and the ice dam capital of the city on north-facing slopes. Midtown and the Harmony corridor were built from the 1980s through the 2000s, mostly architectural asphalt now hitting 20 to 30 years. Fossil Creek, Rigden Farm, Bucking Horse, Maple Hill, and the streets south of Harmony are newer, HOA-governed, and were the first wave to be reroofed under the Class 4 rule after 2019.

The west edge is different. From Overland Trail up to Horsetooth Reservoir and out to Bellvue and LaPorte, homes sit in grass and ponderosa with real ember exposure, and the 2020 Cameron Peak fire put smoke over the city for weeks. For those addresses we talk about Class A assemblies and ember-resistant venting, not just hail.

sections.h2: Wind off the foothills
sections.html: Fort Collins gets the same Chinook downslope winds as the rest of the Front Range. The March 13, 2019 bomb cyclone closed I-25 north of the city and produced gusts of 60 to 80 miles per hour across the region, and the foothill gap at Horsetooth funnels winter wind onto the west side neighborhoods every year. Older three-tab shingles were rated for 60 miles per hour; we install shingles rated to 130 with six nails and a sealed starter and ridge. On the exposed west-side lots we recommend standing seam metal, which handles wind, hail, and embers in one system.

sections.h2: Permits and inspections with Fort Collins Building Services
sections.html:
Every reroof in the city requires a permit from City of Fort Collins Building Services, part of Community Development and Neighborhood Services at 281 North College Avenue. The rules that matter: asphalt shingles must be Class 4 when 50 percent or more of the roof is replaced (a partial repair of 49 percent or less may match the existing material); ice barrier must run from the eave to at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall, or 36 inches up the slope on roofs 8:12 and steeper; attic ventilation must meet the adopted IRC; and every permit closes with a final inspection and a Letter of Completion. City inspectors bring their own ladders and do not need anyone home. Next-day inspections are not available in storm season because of volume, so we build the inspection into the schedule rather than promising a date we cannot hold.

If your home is in a historic district or is a designated landmark, a roof change may need a certificate of appropriateness from Historic Preservation before the building permit issues. We have done that paperwork and know which materials get approved. Addresses outside city limits in LaPorte, Bellvue, and the Horsetooth foothills are permitted through Larimer County, which requires a Class A covering, Class 4 shingles, ice barrier, and a roofing certification.

sections.h2: HOA review in the newer neighborhoods
sections.html: Nearly every subdivision south of Drake Road has an HOA with architectural guidelines. Most specify an approved color range and shingle profile, and since the city already requires Class 4, the HOA review is usually about appearance. Rigden Farm, Fossil Creek, Bucking Horse, and the Harmony corridor communities each have their own process; some approve by email in a week, some only at a monthly meeting. We prepare the packet with product data, the warranty, and a physical sample so your approval is not the thing holding up the install.

sections.h2: Systems, claims, and why Loveland is close enough
sections.html:
For most Fort Collins homes we install a Class 4 architectural shingle on full ice barrier and synthetic underlayment. On Old Town homes that need the right look, synthetic slate and shake carries a Class 4 rating and passes historic review more easily than it used to. For low-slope additions and the flat-roofed mid-century homes near campus, we use membrane rather than forcing shingles. Every job starts with a free photo-documented inspection and a written itemized estimate.

If the roof is a storm claim, our hail damage repair team documents the damage, meets your adjuster after you sign, and works to the approved scope. We never waive deductibles, because Colorado law prohibits it. Our shop is fifteen minutes south on College Avenue or I-25, which means we are on site when the adjuster is, and we are still here when the warranty matters.

faq.q: Does Fort Collins require Class 4 shingles on a repair?
faq.a: It depends on the size of the repair. Under the city roof covering requirements, replacing 50 percent or more of the roof area requires UL 2218 Class 4 asphalt shingles. A partial repair covering 49 percent or less of the roof may use the same or a similar non-impact-resistant shingle. Any addition or patio cover that gets its entire roof replaced must also use Class 4.

faq.q: How much does a roofing permit cost in Fort Collins?
faq.a: City of Fort Collins Building Services charges reroof permit fees based on the project valuation, so a larger or more expensive roof pays more. We list the permit fee as a separate line on the written estimate and handle the application, the final inspection request, and the Letter of Completion. Call Building Services at (970) 416-2740 if you want to confirm a fee directly.

faq.q: My house is in an Old Town historic district. Will that affect my roof?
faq.a: It can. Designated landmarks and homes in historic districts may need a certificate of appropriateness from Historic Preservation before the building permit is issued, and the material and color are reviewed for compatibility. Class 4 architectural shingles in a dark, matte color are routinely approved, and synthetic slate or shake is an option when the original roof was wood or slate. We handle the application.

faq.q: When is hail season in Fort Collins?
faq.a: May through August. The storms that drove the Class 4 ordinance hit in late June of 2014, mid June of 2017, and mid June of 2018, and the July 27, 2022 storm on the east side was the largest since. Afternoon and evening storms are the norm. If you hear hail of an inch or more, schedule an inspection within a couple of weeks rather than waiting for a leak.

faq.q: Do you serve LaPorte, Bellvue, and the Horsetooth foothills?
faq.a: Yes. Those addresses are outside the city and are permitted through Larimer County, which requires a Class A roof covering, Class 4 shingles on replacement roofs, ice barrier to two feet inside the wall, and a roofing certification. Because that area is inside the wildland urban interface, we also talk through ember-resistant vents and noncombustible gutters, which the state wildfire code now expects on many reroofs.

sections.h2: Hail and wind on the Weld County plains
sections.html:
Greeley sits at 4,676 feet at the junction of the Cache la Poudre and South Platte rivers, the seat of Weld County and the lowest elevation of any town we serve. Without the foothills to break them, storms that form over the Front Range arrive here fully built. Weld County regularly leads Colorado in hail reports and has recorded more tornadoes than any county in the country, a fact the city museum itself has written about.

The dates Greeley homeowners remember: June 19, 2018, when golf ball hail piled several inches deep in the city and a swath of baseball hail crossed southern Weld County the same afternoon; July 29, 2018, when 1.75 inch hail hit Greeley and 2 inch hail fell on Evans a few minutes later; the September 11, 2019 evening storm that dropped ping pong ball hail on Greeley and Erie; and the three-day run of May 26 through 28, 2023, with repeated 1.25 to 1.5 inch reports across the city and Severance. More recently, 1.5 inch hail was reported near Lucerne on the north edge on June 20, 2026. Hail season here runs May through August, and a roof in Greeley should be expected to see at least one damaging storm in its lifetime.

sections.h2: What is on Greeley roofs
sections.html:
The oldest roofs are downtown and in the Union Colony era blocks between 8th and 11th Avenues, where 1880s to 1920s houses carry steep pitches, plank decks, and often brick parapets that need proper counterflashing. The University district around UNC is 1920s to 1950s stock, a mix of owner-occupied homes and rentals, many with layered shingles and tired attic ventilation. Central and west Greeley between 23rd and 47th Avenues is 1960s and 1970s ranch and split-level territory: low 4:12 pitches, long overhangs, and roofs that were cheap three-tab until the last storm replaced them. West of 47th Avenue, in Promontory, Kelly Farm, Boomerang, St. Michaels, and Owl Ridge, the homes are 2000s and newer, with architectural shingles and HOAs.

Then there is the commercial inventory, which is bigger here than in any of our other towns. Flat and low-slope TPO, EPDM, and modified bitumen on retail and warehouses along Highway 34 and 10th Street, metal panel on agricultural and industrial buildings along Highway 85, and aging built-up roofs on older buildings downtown. The sun on an open plains roof is punishing, and single-ply membranes here age faster than their brochures suggest.

sections.h2: Roof systems that make sense in Greeley
sections.html:
On houses, a Class 4 impact-resistant architectural shingle with a high-wind nailing pattern is the baseline, because the hail and the plains wind both demand it. Stone-coated steel and metal roofing are the long-term answer on shops, barns, and the newer custom homes on the west side. For commercial owners, we install and repair TPO and EPDM, and we put a lot of value on reflective roof coatings, which extend the life of a sound membrane and cut cooling load on a Greeley summer afternoon. Our commercial roofing work is run with written phasing plans, certificates of insurance, and a safety plan, so a reroof does not shut down your tenants or your loading dock.

Wind matters as much as hail. Plains gusts drive rain under lifted shingles and peel loose membrane edges, so we seal ridges, use six nails, and mechanically fasten membrane perimeters to the manufacturer's high-wind detail.

sections.h2: Permits, inspections, and HOAs in Greeley
sections.html:
Roof replacements inside the city are permitted through the City of Greeley Building Inspection Division at 1100 10th Street, with applications submitted through the city's online portal. The permit card has to be posted on site, and the permit closes only after a final inspection. The city has adopted the 2021 International Residential Code, and we install ice barrier at the eaves and drip edge at eaves and rakes on every job whether or not an inspector asks. Evans and Garden City permit separately, and addresses in unincorporated Weld County go through the county's building department. We identify the jurisdiction from your address before we write the estimate.

HOA review is standard in the west Greeley subdivisions and in the Promontory and Kelly Farm areas, usually a color and profile approval. Metro districts in the newest developments add their own design guidelines. We bring product data and a sample board so the architectural committee can approve on the first pass.

sections.h2: Storm claims without the games
sections.html: After every big Weld County storm, trucks with out-of-state plates show up in Greeley neighborhoods offering to cover the deductible. Colorado law (C.R.S. 6-22-105) prohibits that, and we do not do it. What we do is a free photo-documented inspection, a written itemized estimate, and, once you sign, the adjuster meeting and scope review. If you are not sure whether your roof was hit, this guide to spotting hail damage shows what we look for, and this one explains how long a roof really lasts in Colorado, which on the plains is shorter than the warranty suggests.

sections.h2: Thirty minutes from Loveland, every week
sections.html: Our shop in Loveland is a half hour west on Highway 34, and we have crews in Greeley and Evans every week. For a homeowner that means a real local company with a phone that rings next year. For a property manager it means a roofer who can walk every building in a portfolio, prioritize repairs, and schedule replacements around your budget year. Call (970) 430-5884 or book a free inspection.

faq.a: Yes. Full roof replacement in the city is permitted through the City of Greeley Building Inspection Division, the permit card must be posted on site, and the job is not closed until a final inspection passes. Minor patching of a few shingles does not require a permit. We apply, post the card, and schedule the inspection as part of every job.

faq.q: What does a roofing permit cost in Greeley?
faq.a: The city sets permit fees on a valuation schedule, so a larger or more expensive roof pays a higher fee. We break the permit fee out as its own line in the written estimate rather than hiding it in the total. You can confirm a fee directly with the Building Inspection Division at (970) 350-9830 before you sign anything.

faq.q: Do you handle commercial flat roofs in Greeley?
faq.a: Yes. TPO, EPDM, modified bitumen, metal retrofit, and silicone and acrylic coating systems for retail, industrial, agricultural, and multifamily buildings in Greeley and Evans. We plan phasing and access around your operations, provide certificates of insurance and a safety plan, and can set up a maintenance schedule for a portfolio rather than waiting for leaks.

faq.a: Some do and most at least allow them. The west Greeley subdivisions and the newer metro districts typically require architectural review for color and profile, and several now specify a Class 4 minimum because of the claim history. Many insurers offer a premium credit for Class 4. We check your covenants and prepare the submittal with the product data the committee needs.

sections.h2: The storm that defined Windsor
sections.html:
Just before noon on May 22, 2008, an EF3 tornado with winds estimated up to 165 miles per hour crossed the Town of Windsor, killed one man in his RV, injured 78 people, and generated roughly 24,000 auto and homeowner claims worth about 193.5 million dollars. The President signed a federal disaster declaration four days later. A large share of the roofs in central Windsor date from the rebuild that followed, which means they are now 15 to 18 years old and have taken every hail storm since.

And there have been plenty. Windsor sits at 4,797 feet, straddling the Weld and Larimer county line, directly under one of the most active hail tracks on the Front Range. On June 12, 2017, 2.75 inch hail fell on Severance on the same afternoon that 4.25 inch stones were measured at Pierce. On July 27, 2022, tennis ball and baseball hail, 2.25 to 2.5 inches, came down between Timnath and Severance along the Windsor town line. May 27, 2023 brought 1.25 inch hail to Severance, and the overnight storm of June 16 to 17, 2025 dropped 1.25 to 1.75 inch hail across Timnath, Eaton, and the north side. Hail season is May through August, and in Windsor it rarely skips a year.

sections.h2: Neighborhoods and what is on the roofs
sections.html:
Old town Windsor, around Main Street and Boardwalk Park, is the original 1880s to 1920s town: steep gables, plank decks, and a few brick storefronts with parapets. The 1970s to 1990s streets north and east of downtown are ranches and two-stories with architectural asphalt that has mostly been replaced once already. Water Valley and Pelican Lakes, built from the late 1990s on around the lakes and the golf course, carry the town's premium roofs: concrete tile, standing seam accents, and heavy architectural shingles, all under strict design review. Highland Meadows on the Larimer side has similar golf-course architecture. Jacoby Farm, Windshire Park, Poudre Heights, and Harmony Ridge are 2000s and 2010s production homes with builder-grade shingles now reaching their limit. RainDance, on the west side, is the newest and largest, governed by metro districts with their own design guidelines.

On inspection we see the same pattern across the newer subdivisions: wind-creased shingles on east and south exposures from plains gusts, hail bruising concentrated on the slopes facing the storm track, and sealed-down ridge caps that let go in winter.

sections.h2: Roof systems that fit Windsor
sections.html: Class 4 impact-resistant architectural shingles are the workhorse here, and most Windsor HOAs now either require them or approve them without debate. In Water Valley and Pelican Lakes, where the covenants call for a premium look, we install concrete and clay tile and Class 4 synthetic slate and shake that pass the architectural committee and the hail. On the open east side and on shops and outbuildings toward Severance, standing seam metal handles both the wind and the ice. Every roof gets six-nail high-wind fastening and a sealed ridge, because the 2008 tornado was not the last time Windsor saw real wind.

sections.h2: Permits, inspections, and HOA review in Windsor
sections.html:
Reroofs in town are permitted through the Town of Windsor Community Development department at the Building Permit Desk, 200 North 11th Street, and building inspections are scheduled through the town's third-party inspection provider. The town publishes a residential reroof handout, requires a final inspection to close the permit, and has set the 2025 Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code to take effect in Windsor on July 1, 2026, which mainly affects any mapped interface parcels on the Larimer side. Parts of the Windsor area, including Highland Meadows and the Harmony Road corridor, are in unincorporated Larimer County, which requires a Class A covering, Class 4 shingles on replacement roofs, ice barrier, and a roofing certification. Unincorporated Weld County permits separately. We confirm your jurisdiction from the address before quoting.

HOA and metro district review is a fact of life in Windsor. Water Valley, Pelican Lakes, Highland Meadows, RainDance, and most of the 2000s subdivisions require color and profile approval, several set Class 4 as a minimum, and the golf course communities review tile and metal profiles closely. Colorado law stops an HOA from blocking a less flammable replacement for a wood shake roof and from prohibiting solar. We prepare the submittal with product sheets, warranty, and a sample so the approval arrives before the material does.

sections.html: Windsor gets door-knocked after every storm. Our rule is simple: get a free photo-documented inspection, decide with your agent whether a claim makes sense, and sign with one contractor who will meet the adjuster. Our insurance claim roofing process handles the scope review and supplements. We never pay or waive deductibles, because Colorado law prohibits it. That is what makes hail repair and roof replacement work here: a lead who can be on your roof the morning after the storm, a crew that knows the RainDance and Water Valley design guidelines, and a Loveland phone number that will still answer in five years. Call (970) 430-5884 or book a free inspection.

faq.a: Yes. Reroofing is listed among the project permits issued by the Town of Windsor Community Development department, and the permit closes with a final inspection scheduled through the town inspection line. Minor repairs under about one square generally do not need a permit. We apply at the Building Permit Desk, post the permit, and schedule the inspection as part of the job.

faq.q: Does my Windsor HOA require Class 4 shingles?
faq.a: Many do. Water Valley, Pelican Lakes, Highland Meadows, RainDance, and several of the 2000s subdivisions either require a Class 4 minimum or approve Class 4 without further review, and all of them require color and profile approval. We read your covenants, prepare the architectural submittal, and supply the product documentation your insurer needs for a Class 4 premium credit.

faq.q: When is hail season in Windsor?
faq.a: May through August, with the biggest documented storms in mid June and late July. Severance took 2.75 inch hail on June 12, 2017, the Timnath and Severance side of town saw 2.25 to 2.5 inch hail on July 27, 2022, and the June 2025 overnight storm hit the north side. If you hear hail of an inch or more, schedule an inspection within a couple of weeks.

faq.q: Do you serve Severance and the unincorporated areas around Windsor?
faq.a: Yes. Severance, the Harmony Road corridor, Highland Meadows, and the farm and acreage addresses between Windsor and Fort Collins are all in our everyday range. Those addresses may be permitted through Larimer County or Weld County rather than the town, each with its own roofing requirements, and we confirm the jurisdiction from the address before we write the estimate.

lede: Berthoud wrote its own roofing regulations, and they are stricter than most people expect: Class 4 only, no three-tab, full tear-off, and a certificate of insurance on file before the permit issues. We work to them every week, ten minutes from our shop.
summary: Class 4 replacement, hail and wind repair, and HOA-ready roofing in Berthoud, Campion, and the Highway 287 corridor, with town permits handled.

sections.h2: Berthoud roofing rules, in plain language
sections.html:
Start with the regulations, because in Berthoud they decide the product before you do. The Town of Berthoud Planning and Building Department at 807 Mountain Avenue has adopted the 2024 International Residential Code and publishes its own roofing regulations. The highlights: a building permit is required for anything over one square of shingles, and the permit card must be posted on the house before work starts. Asphalt shingles must be Class 4 impact resistant, tested to UL 2218. Three-tab shingles are not allowed; dimensional shingles only. All existing roofing must be torn off, with one exception for a single layer of asphalt under new asphalt, and no roof with two or more existing layers may be covered. Ice barrier and drip edge are required, damaged sheathing, jacks, vents, and flashing must be replaced, and the roofer has to file a certificate of insurance with the application. Tile roofs and commercial flat roofs get a mid-roof inspection before the final.

Addresses outside town limits, including Campion, the Carter Lake foothills, and the acreages along Highway 56 and County Road 17, fall under Larimer County, which requires a Class A covering countywide, Class 4 asphalt shingles, ice barrier to two feet inside the wall, and a roofing certification. The small slice of Berthoud in Weld County permits through the county. We confirm the jurisdiction before quoting.

sections.h2: What Berthoud roofs are up against
sections.html:
Berthoud sits at 5,033 feet in Larimer County, between the Little Thompson River and the Carter Lake hogback, and the weather arrives from both directions. Hail comes off the foothills in the afternoon: 1.75 inch hail was reported in Berthoud on May 22, 2008, the same day the Windsor tornado, 1.25 inch hail fell south of town on July 20, 2024, and the evening of June 24, 2026 brought repeated golf ball reports, 1.5 to 1.75 inches, around Berthoud. The Front Range hail season runs May through August.

Wind comes off the hogback in winter. The 100 mile per hour gust recorded just north of Carter Lake on the night of January 6 to 7, 2020 was measured a few miles west of town, and the same downslope flow lifts shingles on every west-facing slope from Berthoud Lake to Heron Lakes. Snow sits longer on the north sides here than it does in Loveland, and ice dams on under-ventilated eaves are a January problem we repair every year.

sections.h2: Neighborhoods and roof types
sections.html:
Downtown Berthoud, along Mountain Avenue and the blocks around the 1880s railroad grid, has the town's oldest roofs: steep Victorian and bungalow pitches on plank decks, often with wood shake still buried under asphalt. The 1970s to 1990s streets around Berthoud Lake and south of Highway 56 are ranches and split-levels with their second or third asphalt roof. The growth since 2015 is where most of the work is: Heron Lakes and TPC Colorado, the lakeside golf community on the northwest side, with tile, standing seam, and heavy Class 4 shingles under a design review board; Hammond Farm, Prairie Star, Rose Farm, Vantage, and Mary's Farm on the east and south sides, with production builder shingles that will see their first damaging hail before they are 20 years old.

What we see most often on inspection: builder-grade shingles with four nails on a six-nail wind zone, missing ice barrier on homes built before the current code, and hail bruising on the east and south slopes that were facing the June storms.

sections.h2: Roof systems that make sense here
sections.html: Because the town requires Class 4, the conversation in Berthoud is about which Class 4 system and how it is installed. For most homes that is a Class 4 architectural shingle on full ice barrier and synthetic underlayment with six-nail fastening and sealed ridge. In Heron Lakes and TPC Colorado we install concrete tile and standing seam metal to the community design guidelines, with the mid-roof inspection the town requires on tile. On the acreages and shops along Highway 56 and toward Campion, metal panel roofing is the right call for wind and snow. Older downtown homes that want the look of the original wood get Class 4 synthetic shake, which the town accepts and insurers prefer. Read our Class 4 and insurance discount guide before choosing a shingle line.

sections.h2: HOAs and hail claims
sections.html: The Heron Lakes and TPC Colorado HOA design committees review color, profile, and material, and most of the newer east-side subdivision HOAs require at least a color approval. We bring the submittal with product data and a sample board. If the roof is a storm claim, our hail damage repair team documents it with photos, meets the adjuster after you sign, and works to the approved scope. Colorado law prohibits paying or waiving deductibles and we never do. New construction warranty questions are common in Berthoud: builder warranties cover workmanship for a limited time and exclude storm damage, and we will tell you honestly which bucket your roof is in.

sections.h2: Ten minutes down Highway 287
sections.html: Our shop is ten minutes north of Berthoud on Highway 287, which is why we treat the town as our own backyard. A roof replacement here gets the same crew lead from inspection through final, the permit and certificate of insurance filed with the town, and a written itemized estimate before anything is ordered. Call (970) 430-5884 or book a free inspection.

faq.q: Does Berthoud allow three-tab shingles?
faq.a: No. The Town of Berthoud roofing regulations permit dimensional shingles only, and every asphalt shingle must be Class 4 impact resistant tested to UL 2218. The regulations also require full tear-off except for a single existing asphalt layer, ice barrier, drip edge, and replacement of damaged sheathing and flashing. We install to the town standard on every Berthoud roof.

faq.q: What does a roofing permit cost in Berthoud?
faq.a: The Town of Berthoud Planning and Building Department sets its own fee schedule and the roofing regulations do not publish a flat rate, so the fee depends on the project. We list the permit fee as a separate line on the written estimate and file the application, the certificate of insurance the town requires, and the inspection request. You can confirm a fee with the department at (970) 532-2643.

faq.q: Does Heron Lakes or TPC Colorado require a specific roof?
faq.a: The design guidelines in Heron Lakes and TPC Colorado review material, profile, and color, and the approved palette favors tile, standing seam, and heavy architectural Class 4 shingles. Approval comes from the architectural review committee, not the town, and it is separate from the building permit. We prepare the submittal with product sheets and samples so the committee can approve it on the first pass.

faq.q: When is hail season in Berthoud?
faq.a: May through August on the northern Front Range. Documented Berthoud reports include 1.75 inch hail on May 22, 2008, 1.25 inch hail on July 20, 2024, and golf ball hail on June 24, 2026. The afternoon storms build over the foothills west of Carter Lake and move east across town, so west and central Berthoud often take the first hit of a given storm.

lede: Longmont is where the hail belt meets Boulder County wildfire rules, and where a lot of 1970s cedar shake is still waiting to be replaced. We roof the St. Vrain valley from Old Town to Prospect to the Weld County side.
summary: Hail repair, Class 4 and metal replacement, and cedar-to-synthetic conversions in Longmont, Niwot, Hygiene, and the Carbon Valley, with city permits closed.

sections.h2: The St. Vrain valley from the roof
sections.html:
Longmont sits at 4,981 feet on the St. Vrain River in Boulder County, with its east side spilling into Weld County and Longs Peak filling the western sky. It is the southernmost town we serve from Loveland, 25 minutes down Highway 287, and it has the most varied housing stock of any of them.

Old Town and the East Side historic district are 1870s to 1920s homes on the original Chicago-Colorado Colony grid: steep pitches, plank decks, box gutters, and dormers that leak at the cheek walls. Southmoor Park, Loomiller, and the streets west of Hover were built in the 1960s and 1970s, and this is cedar shake country; many of those ranches and split-levels still carry wood roofs or asphalt laid over them. Prospect New Town, on the south side, is a 1990s and 2000s new urbanist neighborhood with standing seam metal, flat roofs, and modern details that need a roofer who understands membrane and metal, not just shingles. Clover Basin, Meadowview, Fox Hill, and Harvest Junction are 1990s to 2010s production neighborhoods on architectural asphalt. Niwot and Hygiene to the west, and Mead, Firestone, and Frederick to the east, are small-lot and acreage addresses under county or neighboring-town jurisdiction.

sections.h2: Hail, wind, and the 2013 flood
sections.html:
Longmont takes Front Range hail every year. The reporting network has logged 2.5 inch hail in the Longmont area in the past decade, 1.5 inch hail at Erie on May 30, 2024, and 1.5 to 1.75 inch hail just north of town around Berthoud on June 24, 2026. The September 2013 flood put the St. Vrain through downtown and damaged hundreds of homes, and some of those roofs were patched quickly and never properly replaced. Hail season runs May through August, and the storms tend to track from the foothills east across the city along Highway 66 and Highway 119.

Wind is a Boulder County problem in its own right. Chinook downslope winds off the Indian Peaks regularly exceed 70 miles per hour at the foothills, and the December 30, 2021 wind event that drove the Marshall Fire through south Boulder County produced gusts over 100 miles per hour. That day is also why wildfire resiliency is now part of every roofing conversation in the county, not only for mountain addresses. Here are the roofing materials that make sense in Colorado wildfire zones.

sections.h2: Permits and inspections with City of Longmont Building Inspection
sections.html:
Reroofs in the city are permitted through City of Longmont Building Inspection, and the city publishes detailed roofing guidelines. Repairs of 100 square feet or less need no permit; anything larger triggers full replacement of the roof, not just the damaged plane. Overlays are not allowed; every existing layer comes off. Shingles must be rated for 110 mile per hour wind, which rules out standard three-tab on a house. Ice and water shield is required, drip edge is required at both eaves and rakes, rusted or damaged flashings and vents must be replaced, and attic ventilation must meet the city formula unless the roof is a closed, condensation-controlled assembly. Mid-roof inspections are not required on residential pitched roofs, so the job closes on a final. Commercial built-up roofs require a mid-roof inspection and a city Class D-2 license.

Addresses in unincorporated Boulder County, including Hygiene, Niwot, and the foothill acreages toward Lyons, follow Boulder County building rules that restrict wood shake in wildfire zones and now carry the Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code, which requires a Class A covering when 25 percent or more of a roof is replaced in a mapped interface area. Mead, Firestone, Frederick, and Erie each permit separately. We confirm the jurisdiction from your address before we quote.

sections.h2: HOA review and the cedar shake question
sections.html: Prospect has strict design covenants on material and color, and most of the 1990s and later subdivisions on the south and west sides require architectural approval. Some older covenants in Southmoor Park and the west side still reference cedar shake, but Colorado law (C.R.S. 38-33.3-106.5) prohibits an HOA from blocking a homeowner who wants to replace a wood shake roof with a less flammable covering. That is the single most common Longmont conversation we have: the homeowner wants the shake look without the fire risk and the insurance surcharge. The answer is usually Class A, Class 4 synthetic shake, which keeps the profile, satisfies the HOA, and passes both the hail and the fire test. Where a client insists on real wood, our cedar shake roofing page explains where fire-treated shake is still permitted and what it costs to maintain.

sections.h2: Roof systems for Longmont
sections.html: For the production neighborhoods, a Class 4 architectural shingle rated to 130 miles per hour, on ice and water shield with six-nail fastening, is the right baseline and earns the insurance credit. In Prospect and on modern custom homes we install standing seam metal and single-ply membrane on the flat sections. On Old Town homes, synthetic slate or a heavy architectural shingle in a historic color keeps the look. For foothill addresses west of Hover and toward Lyons, we build Class A assemblies with ember-resistant venting and noncombustible gutters. Every job starts with a free photo-documented roof inspection and a written itemized estimate.

sections.h2: Storm claims and a roofer who stays
sections.html: After a St. Vrain valley hail storm, our hail damage repair team inspects first and recommends a claim only when the damage supports one. We meet the adjuster once you sign, and we never pay or waive deductibles because Colorado law prohibits it. Longmont is a 25 minute drive from our shop, close enough that we are here for the inspection, the install, and the warranty call years later. Call (970) 430-5884 or book a free inspection.

faq.q: Can I replace my cedar shake roof in Longmont with cedar again?
faq.a: Inside the city, fire-treated wood shake is still a permitted covering on most lots, but the cost, the maintenance, and the insurance surcharge make it a hard case. In unincorporated Boulder County wildfire zones and mapped interface areas under the state wildfire code, a Class A covering is required when a quarter or more of the roof is replaced. Most clients choose Class A synthetic shake, which keeps the look.

faq.q: Does Longmont require a permit for a roof repair?
faq.a: Repairs of 100 square feet or less do not need a permit. Anything larger requires a permit from City of Longmont Building Inspection and, under the city guidelines, triggers replacement of the full roof rather than a patch. Overlays are not allowed. A homeowner may pull the permit on a primary residence they will roof themselves; otherwise the contractor pulls it. We handle it either way.

faq.q: Will my Longmont HOA let me install a metal roof?
faq.a: It depends on the covenants. Prospect and several newer communities approve standing seam in specific colors and profiles, while some older subdivisions limit roofs to shingle or shake profiles. HOAs cannot block solar or a less flammable replacement for wood shake under Colorado law. We read your covenants and prepare the submittal with samples so the committee can approve it without a second meeting.

faq.q: When is hail season in Longmont?
faq.a: May through August, with June and July the most active months. Recent reports within the Longmont reporting area include 1.5 inch hail at Erie on May 30, 2024 and golf ball hail around Berthoud on June 24, 2026. Storms generally build over the foothills and move east across the city, so the west side often sees hail first. Schedule an inspection within a couple of weeks of any storm with inch-plus hail.

lede: Johnstown has grown faster than almost any town in Colorado, which means thousands of first-generation builder roofs sitting under the busiest hail track in Weld County. We are ten minutes east on Highway 402 and we are here every week.
summary: Hail repair, Class 4 replacement, and metro district roofing in Johnstown and Milliken, from Thompson River Ranch to old town, with permits handled.

sections.h2: A young town with a lot of first roofs
sections.html:
Johnstown went from 17,303 residents at the 2020 census to an estimated 22,433 in 2025, and the roofs tell that story. Outside of old town along Parish Avenue, where the 1900s to 1950s homes carry their third or fourth asphalt roof, nearly everything in Johnstown was built after 2000. Rolling Hills Ranch, Pioneer Ridge, Clearview, and Carlson Farm came in the 2000s; Thompson River Ranch, Thompson Crossing, Johnstown Farms, Mountain View, and Ledge Rock filled in through the 2010s and 2020s; and the 2534 corridor at I-25 and Highway 34 added retail, hotel, industrial, and multifamily roofs by the acre. Most of those homes went up with the shingle the builder got the best price on, nailed four per course, and they are now 10 to 20 years into a 25 year rating under Weld County sun and hail.

The town sits at 4,994 feet, mostly in Weld County with a slice in Larimer, on the open plain between the Big Thompson and Little Thompson rivers. There is nothing between a Johnstown roof and the weather.

sections.h2: Hail history in Johnstown and Milliken
sections.html:
The overnight storm of June 16 to 17, 2025 is the one people here still talk about: 2.75 inch hail was measured at Milliken, just east of Johnstown, and the morning brought shattered car windows, stripped trees, and a wave of roof claims across both towns. Before that, 1 inch hail was logged in Johnstown on June 28, 2013, and on June 19, 2018 a swath of baseball hail crossed southern Weld County while golf ball stones piled up in Greeley. Southern Weld County is on the receiving end of storms that form over the foothills and mature as they cross Larimer County, so the hail that reaches Johnstown is often larger than what fell on Loveland an hour earlier. Hail season runs May through August. Here is what to do in the first week after a hail storm.

Wind is the quieter problem. Open-plains gusts crease shingles on east and south exposures and lift ridge caps that were sealed in cold weather. The March 13, 2019 bomb cyclone pushed 60 to 80 mile per hour gusts across the whole region, and a four-nail builder roof does not hold at that speed.

sections.h2: Roof systems that fit Johnstown
sections.html: On a production home the right replacement is a Class 4 impact-resistant architectural shingle with six-nail high-wind fastening, full ice barrier at the eaves, and a sealed ridge. It satisfies the metro district guidelines, earns a premium credit with many insurers, and will outlast the builder shingle it replaces by a wide margin. Read our Class 4 shingle guide for how the insurance discount works. On shops, barns, and the agricultural buildings between Johnstown and Milliken we install metal panel roofing. On the 2534 corridor, our commercial roofing team handles TPO, EPDM, and coatings for retail, multifamily, and light industrial, with phasing plans that keep tenants open.

sections.h2: Permits, inspections, and metro district approvals
sections.html:
Reroofs inside town limits are permitted through the Town of Johnstown Building Department at 39 South Parish Avenue, which operates with a third-party building services provider. The town has adopted the 2018 International Residential Code, applications go through the online portal, the permit card must be posted on site, and the permit closes only after a final inspection. Minor patching of a few shingles does not need a permit; a full replacement does. Milliken permits through its own town building department, and addresses outside either town fall under Weld County or, on the west edge, Larimer County, which requires a Class A covering, Class 4 shingles, ice barrier, and a roofing certification. We confirm jurisdiction from the address.

Nearly every subdivision in Johnstown sits inside a metro district, an HOA, or both, and the town itself notes that HOA architectural approval is separate from the building permit. Thompson River Ranch, Johnstown Farms, Pioneer Ridge, and the others publish color palettes and material lists, and several have adopted a Class 4 minimum since the 2025 storm. We prepare the submittal with product data and a sample so the review happens once.

sections.h2: Storm claims in a storm chaser town
sections.html: Johnstown gets canvassed hard after every storm. Our hail damage repair process starts with a free photo-documented inspection and an honest answer about whether a claim is worth filing. Once you sign, we meet the adjuster, review the scope, and submit supplements with photos. We never pay or waive deductibles, because Colorado law (C.R.S. 6-22-105) prohibits it. If you are being told otherwise by someone at your door, that is the tell.

sections.h2: Ten minutes from our door
sections.html: Our shop on East 3rd Street in Loveland is ten minutes from Johnstown by Highway 402 or Highway 34, and we have crews in Thompson River Ranch and the east-side subdivisions every week. For a roof replacement that means a crew lead who sees the roof at inspection, at install, and at the final, and a local phone number that answers in five years. Call (970) 430-5884 or book a free inspection.

faq.q: Do I need a permit to replace my roof in Johnstown?
faq.a: Yes. Full roof replacement is permitted through the Town of Johnstown Building Department, the permit card must be posted on site, and the permit closes with a final inspection. Patching a few shingles does not require one. Your HOA or metro district approval is a separate step from the town permit. We apply, post the card, schedule the inspection, and prepare the HOA submittal as part of the job.

faq.q: How much is a roofing permit in Johnstown?
faq.a: The town building department sets fees by project valuation, so a larger roof pays a higher fee, and plan review runs roughly two weeks for most residential permits. We show the permit fee as its own line on the written estimate so nothing is buried in the total. You can confirm a fee directly with the Building Department at (970) 587-4664 before signing.

faq.q: Does Thompson River Ranch require Class 4 shingles?
faq.a: Thompson River Ranch and most of the Johnstown metro districts require architectural review of color and profile, and several have added a Class 4 minimum after the June 2025 hail. Even where it is not required, Class 4 is the right choice on an open-plains roof and most insurers offer a premium credit for it. We read your guidelines and prepare the submittal with the documentation the committee and your carrier need.

faq.q: Do you work in Milliken and the unincorporated county areas?
faq.a: Yes. Milliken, Hill-N-Park, the farm and acreage addresses along Weld County Roads 17 and 42, and the west edge in Larimer County are all in our weekly range. Milliken permits through its own building department and the county addresses through Weld County or Larimer County, each with different roofing rules. We confirm the jurisdiction from your address before writing the estimate.

lede: North of Fort Collins the ground opens up toward Wyoming, and the wind decides which roofs last. Wellington roofs get installed for the exposure first and the hail second.
summary: Wind-rated and Class 4 roofing, metal for barns and shops, and hail repair in Wellington, Waverly, and northern Larimer County, with permits handled.

sections.h2: Wind first, then everything else
sections.html:
Wellington sits at 5,194 feet in northern Larimer County, the highest of the plains towns we serve and the one with the least shelter. The Laramie Foothills stand off to the west and Wyoming is twenty miles north, and the wind between them has nothing to slow it down. The Town of Wellington's own reroof checklist calls for shingle fastening to meet a 115 mile per hour ultimate wind speed in Exposure C and six nails per shingle in high-wind areas. That is not a formality here. The March 13, 2019 bomb cyclone closed I-25 at Wellington under 60 to 80 mile per hour gusts and drifting snow, and ordinary winter Chinooks peel ridge caps off under-nailed roofs in Buffalo Creek and Wellington Downs every year.

Hail comes too. The National Weather Service has logged 1.75 inch hail in Wellington on August 22, 2007, August 14, 2008, August 3, 2013, and June 19, 2018, the last of those in the same evening that golf ball stones hit Fort Collins and LaPorte. Notice the dates: Wellington's big storms skew to late summer, so the hail season here really runs May through August with August as dangerous as June.

sections.h2: Wellington roofs, from Cleveland Avenue to the county roads
sections.html:
Old town Wellington, on the grid around Cleveland Avenue, is 1900s to 1940s stock: small gabled houses, a few brick commercial roofs with parapets, and plank decks that have been reroofed many times. The 1990s and 2000s growth south and east of downtown, Wellington Downs, Buffalo Creek, Harvest Village, Sage Meadows, and The Knolls, is production housing on architectural asphalt, and the first wave of those roofs is hitting 20 to 25 years. The newest streets near Boxelder Creek went up with better shingles but the same four-nail habit. Outside town, Waverly and the acreages along County Roads 7, 9, and 62 add a different roof entirely: barns, shops, hay sheds, and steel-framed outbuildings with screw-down metal panel, often with fasteners that have backed out and trim that the wind has worked loose.

What we find on inspection: wind creases on west and north slopes, lifted and resealed ridge caps, hail bruising on east slopes, and on the ag buildings, loose panels and failed closures at the ridge and eave.

sections.h2: Roof systems that survive here
sections.html: On houses, a Class 4 impact-resistant architectural shingle rated to 130 miles per hour, six nails per shingle, sealed starter and ridge, and full ice barrier at the eaves. The wind rating matters more than it does in Loveland. On the acreages and anywhere the owner wants to stop thinking about the roof, standing seam metal with concealed clips is the right answer: no exposed fasteners to back out, a Class 4 impact rating, and a wind rating that exceeds anything the plains will deliver. For barns and shops we repair and replace screw-down metal panel roofing with proper closures, butyl tape, and trim that is fastened to stay. Here is how long each system really lasts in Colorado, which on an exposed Wellington lot is at the short end of every range.

sections.h2: Permits, inspections, and HOA approvals in Wellington
sections.html:
Reroofs inside town limits are permitted through the Town of Wellington Building Department, with plan review, permits, and inspections run through the town's third-party building services partner and its online portal. The town checklist is specific: a permit is required for anything over one square of shingles; a detached garage or shed roof over 120 square feet needs its own permit; permits are valid for 180 days; ice barrier is required at the eaves; a final inspection is required on every roof; and tile, metal, and other non-asphalt roofs get a mid-roof inspection as well. The permit has to be posted where it can be seen from the street, the contractor has to provide a secured ladder, and photos are not accepted for reinspection. Every contractor working in town must hold a Town of Wellington contractor license, which we do.

Waverly and the county road addresses are permitted through Larimer County, which requires a Class A covering, Class 4 asphalt shingles on replacement roofs, ice barrier to two feet inside the wall, a roofing certification form, and attachment rated for the site wind speed, which across much of northern Larimer County is 140 miles per hour or more. Buffalo Creek, Wellington Downs, and the newer subdivisions carry HOA color and profile review, and the town checklist itself reminds homeowners to check with the HOA before applying. We prepare the submittal.

sections.h2: Hail claims, done straight
sections.html: When a storm comes through, our hail damage repair team walks the roof, photographs every slope, and tells you whether the damage supports a claim. Wind damage is often the bigger finding here, and storm damage roofing covers the creased shingles, lifted ridges, and torn metal that a hail-only adjuster can miss. After you sign, we meet the adjuster and work to the approved scope. We never pay or waive deductibles, because Colorado law prohibits it.

sections.h2: Thirty-five minutes up I-25, worth the drive
sections.html: Wellington is 35 minutes north of our Loveland shop, and we schedule it in blocks so a crew is in town for days at a time rather than a single trip. A roof replacement here comes with the town permit, the ladder for the inspector, a written itemized estimate, and a Loveland phone number that will still answer when you have a question in five years. Call (970) 430-5884 or book a free inspection.

faq.q: Do you roof barns, shops, and outbuildings around Wellington?
faq.a: Yes. Metal panel repair and replacement on barns, shops, hay sheds, and steel-framed outbuildings in Waverly and along the county roads is regular work for us. That includes replacing backed-out fasteners, closures, and wind-damaged trim on screw-down panel, and full replacement with standing seam where the owner wants a roof that does not need attention. A separate permit is needed in town for any secondary roof over 120 square feet.

faq.q: Does Larimer County require Class 4 shingles outside Wellington town limits?
faq.a: Yes. Larimer County requires Class 4 impact-rated asphalt shingles on new and replacement roofs, a Class A roof covering countywide, ice barrier from the eave to at least two feet inside the exterior wall, and a signed roofing certification. Much of northern Larimer County is also a high-wind design area, so the roof covering has to be attached to the manufacturer detail for the site wind speed.

faq.q: What does a roofing permit cost in Wellington?
faq.a: The Town of Wellington sets permit fees on its own schedule through its building services partner, and the reroof checklist does not publish a flat rate, so the fee depends on the project. We list the permit fee as its own line on the written estimate and handle the application, the posting, the inspector ladder, and the final inspection. You can confirm a fee with the town at (970) 568-3381.

faq.q: When is hail season in Wellington?
faq.a: May through August, and in Wellington the late-summer storms have historically been as bad as the June ones. Documented golf ball hail hit the town in late August 2007, mid August 2008, early August 2013, and mid June 2018. Schedule an inspection within a couple of weeks of any storm with inch-plus hail, and after any wind event that leaves shingle tabs in the yard.
