sections.h2: The newest roofs in Northern Colorado, and the storm that tested them
sections.html:
Timnath was a farm town of 625 people at the 2010 census, 6,487 in 2020, and an estimated 10,848 by 2024, the fastest-growing town in Colorado in 2022. Outside the handful of 1880s to 1950s houses along Main Street in old Timnath, every roof in town was installed after 2005 and most after 2015. That makes Timnath the clearest test of builder-grade roofing anywhere in the region, and the test came on the evening of July 27, 2022, when an off-duty weather service employee measured tennis ball to baseball hail, 2.25 to 2.5 inches, between Timnath and Severance. Roofs that were three years old had to be replaced.

It was not the first time. On June 24, 2014, 2.5 inch hail hit Timnath and east Fort Collins, and on August 3, 2013 and June 12, 2017 golf ball hail was logged in town. More recently, 1.25 inch hail fell on May 27, 2023 and again in the early morning of June 17, 2025. Timnath sits at 4,869 feet in Larimer County, east of I-25 on the Poudre River bottom, and the cells that mature over Fort Collins arrive here at full strength. Hail season runs May through August.

sections.h2: Neighborhoods, metro districts, and what is on the roofs
sections.html:
Timnath Ranch is the largest neighborhood, 2000s and 2010s production homes under a metro district with published design guidelines. WildWing, around the lakes on the east side, carries a higher-end mix of architectural shingle, stone-coated steel, and standing seam accents. Harmony Club, the golf community south of Harmony Road, has the most premium roofs in town, with concrete tile and heavy designer shingles under a strict architectural review. Serratoga Falls, Timnath Lakes, Rendezvous, and Trailside are the 2015 to 2024 wave, mostly architectural asphalt with four-nail builder installation, and the custom homes along the river and the acreages toward Severance add metal and tile.

What we find on inspection in Timnath: shingles that pass a visual check from the ground but show mat fractures from the 2022 storm when you look closely; wind-lifted shingles on the east exposures where the open plains start; and attic ventilation that met the minimum on paper and not in practice, which shows up as ice dams on north eaves in January. Here is how we tell hail bruising from manufacturing defects on a young roof.

sections.h2: Roof systems that make sense in Timnath
sections.html: For a production home, the upgrade from the builder shingle to a Class 4 impact-resistant architectural shingle with six-nail fastening and full ice barrier is the single best investment on the house. It is what Fort Collins requires next door, what Larimer County requires outside town limits, what most Timnath metro districts approve without debate, and what earns the insurance credit. In WildWing and Harmony Club we install concrete tile, Class 4 synthetic slate and shake, and standing seam metal to the community design guidelines. Stone-coated steel is a strong fit for homeowners who want a shingle look that will not need replacing after the next storm.

sections.h2: Permits, inspections, and HOA approvals in Timnath
sections.html:
Reroofs in town are permitted through Town of Timnath Building Services, part of the Community Development department, with plan review and inspections run through the town's third-party building services provider and its online portal. The town publishes a residential reroof guide based on the 2018 International Residential Code, the permit card has to be posted, and every roof closes with a final inspection. Addresses outside town limits toward Severance and along the river are permitted through Larimer County, which requires a Class A covering, Class 4 asphalt shingles on replacement roofs, ice barrier to two feet inside the wall, and a roofing certification.

Nearly every Timnath subdivision sits inside a metro district, an HOA, or both, and those approvals are separate from the town permit. Timnath Ranch, WildWing, Harmony Club, and the newer communities each publish color palettes and material lists, and the premium neighborhoods review tile and metal profiles closely. Colorado law prevents an HOA from prohibiting solar or a less flammable replacement for wood shake. We prepare the submittal with product sheets, warranty, and a physical sample so the review happens once.

sections.h2: Claims on a young roof
sections.html: Timnath homeowners often hear two things after a storm: the builder saying the roof is under warranty, and a canvasser saying it is totaled. Builder warranties cover workmanship for a limited period and exclude storm damage, so hail is an insurance matter, not a warranty one. Our hail damage repair team inspects first, photographs every slope, and gives you an honest read on whether a claim is worth filing. After you sign, we meet the adjuster and work to the scope. We never pay or waive deductibles, because Colorado law prohibits it, and our insurance claim roofing page explains how the process actually runs.

sections.h2: Twenty minutes from Loveland
sections.html: Timnath is twenty minutes from our shop by I-25 and Harmony Road, and we are in Timnath Ranch and WildWing every week. A roof replacement here comes with the town permit, the metro district submittal, a written itemized estimate, and a Loveland phone number that will still answer in five years. Call (970) 430-5884 or book a free inspection.

faq.q: Will my Timnath metro district or HOA approve a metal or synthetic roof?
faq.a: Most Timnath communities approve stone-coated steel and Class 4 synthetic slate or shake in approved colors, and several approve standing seam in specific profiles. Harmony Club and WildWing review material and profile closely. The approval is separate from the town building permit. We read your design guidelines and prepare the submittal with product sheets and a sample so the committee can approve it at one meeting.

faq.q: Do you offer Class 4 shingles in Timnath?
faq.a: Yes, and it is our standard recommendation on every Timnath roof. Class 4 impact-resistant shingles are required next door in Fort Collins and on Larimer County addresses outside town limits, most metro districts approve them without debate, and many insurers give a premium credit for them. On a town that took 2.5 inch hail in 2022, the upgrade from a builder shingle pays for itself.

faq.q: What does a roofing permit cost in Timnath?
faq.a: Town of Timnath Building Services sets reroof permit fees on its own schedule, so the fee depends on the project. We show the permit fee as its own line on the written estimate, file the application through the town portal, post the card, and schedule the final inspection. You can confirm a fee with the Building Permit Technician at (970) 449-4639 before you sign.

faq.q: My Timnath home is only a few years old. Is hail damage a builder warranty issue?
faq.a: Almost never. Builder workmanship warranties cover installation defects for a limited period and specifically exclude storm damage, so hail and wind damage on a young roof is an insurance claim. We inspect first, document the damage with photos, and tell you plainly whether what we found is storm damage, an installation defect, or normal wear, and which path, if any, makes sense.

name: Estes Park
permitAuthority: Town of Estes Park Community Development, Building Safety Division
title: Estes Park Roofing Contractor
description: Estes Park roofing contractor for Class A metal and synthetic roofs built for wind, snow load, ice dams, and embers. Get a free inspection.
lede: At 7,522 feet, an Estes Park roof has to survive hurricane-force wind, a 70 pound snow load, ice dams every winter, and wind-driven embers. We build mountain roofs like engineered systems, because here they are.
summary: Wind-rated, Class A metal and synthetic roofing for Estes Park, Glen Haven, Drake, and the Big Thompson Canyon, built for snow, ice, and ember exposure.

sections.h2: Four loads, one roof
sections.html:
Estes Park sits at 7,522 feet in southwestern Larimer County, at the mouth of the valley where the Big Thompson and Fall River come together below Rocky Mountain National Park. A roof on the plains has to handle hail and wind. A roof here has to handle wind that strips shingles in sheets, snow that sits for months, ice that works up under every eave, and, since 2020, embers.

The wind is not a figure of speech. On February 18, 2016, a 97 mile per hour gust was recorded two miles northwest of Glen Haven, and the same storm blew car windows out around Estes Park. In November 2011, winds toppled 30-inch-diameter healthy trees and took down power lines across Allenspark and the Estes Valley. Gusts above 70 miles per hour were recorded near Glen Haven again in January 2020. Larimer County classifies the mountain area as a high-wind zone of 140 miles per hour or more, and the county's 2024 code amendments set the minimum design snow load at 70 pounds per square foot between 7,001 and 8,000 feet, with engineered design required above 8,000 feet. Hail is lighter than on the plains but not absent: 1.75 inch hail was logged in Estes Park on July 12, 2007, and the county still requires Class 4 asphalt shingles. Hail season runs May through August.

sections.h2: Wildfire and the 2020 fires
sections.html:
In October 2020, the two largest wildfires in Colorado history burned on both sides of the Estes Valley at the same time. The Cameron Peak fire came down the Poudre and into the Glen Haven and Drake drainages. The East Troublesome fire ran 18 miles in a single day, crossed the Continental Divide inside the national park on October 21, and forced the evacuation of most of the Estes Valley on October 22. Firefighters and a weather change on October 24 and 25 stopped it short of town. Nearly 30,000 acres of the park burned.

That is why roofing here is now a wildfire question first. The Town of Estes Park and Larimer County both sit inside the wildland urban interface, and the 2025 Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code, enforced locally since July 1, 2026, requires a Class A roof covering or assembly on new construction and whenever 25 percent or more of a roof is replaced in a mapped interface area. Attic and rafter vents must be covered with noncombustible 1/8 inch mesh or be ember-tested, and gutters and downspouts must be noncombustible. Larimer County has required a Class A covering across the mountain area for years. Natural cedar shake, which still covers many 1960s to 1980s cabins in Carriage Hills, Little Valley, and along Fall River Road, does not meet any of it. Here are the roofing materials that make sense in Colorado wildfire zones.

sections.h2: Snow load and ice dams
sections.html: Snow at this elevation stacks instead of melting. North slopes in Windcliff and on Prospect Mountain carry a snowpack from December into March, and afternoon melt refreezes at the cold eave into a dam that backs water up under the covering. The fix is a system: full-coverage ice and water membrane on the lower slopes and valleys, not just the two feet the county minimum requires; balanced ventilation so the deck stays cold; and on metal roofs, engineered snow retention laid out on a drawing so a slab does not come off above a door or a deck. Our mountain roofing guide covers snow load and ice dams in detail.

sections.h2: Roof systems that belong in Estes Park
sections.html: Mechanically seamed standing seam metal is the roof we recommend most in the Estes Valley: Class A, Class 4, rated for the wind, sheds snow, and resists embers. Where the architecture or the HOA calls for a shake or slate look, Class A synthetic shake and slate keeps the character of a Fall River cabin without the fire risk, and stone-coated steel does the same with a shingle profile. On the historic buildings downtown and around the Stanley Hotel district, the covering has to pass historic review as well as the fire code, and we have done both. Every attachment is designed for the site wind speed, every eave gets a sealed metal drip and ice membrane, and every vent is ember-resistant. Our metal roofing page explains the panel and finish options.

sections.h2: Permits, inspections, and HOA review in Estes Park
sections.html:
Reroofs inside town limits are permitted through the Town of Estes Park Community Development department's Building Safety division, which has contracted its building services through a third-party provider since 2020. Applications and inspection requests go through the town's online portal, and the office is in Town Hall Room 230 at 170 MacGregor Avenue. Addresses outside town, including Glen Haven, Drake, Allenspark, Pinewood Springs, and the Big Thompson Canyon, are permitted through the Larimer County Building Division, which requires a Class A covering, Class 4 asphalt shingles, ice barrier to two feet inside the wall, attachment rated for the 140 mile per hour design wind, and a signed roofing certification. Both jurisdictions enforce the state wildfire code on reroofs that cross the 25 percent threshold. We confirm the jurisdiction and the interface classification for your parcel before we quote.

HOA and design review is common in Windcliff, Carriage Hills, Little Valley, and the newer communities around Mary's Lake. Older covenants sometimes still reference wood shake, but Colorado law (C.R.S. 38-33.3-106.5) prohibits an HOA from blocking a less flammable replacement, and the wildfire code now overrides any covenant that would require it. We prepare the submittal with product data and samples.

sections.h2: Why a Loveland roofer makes sense up the canyon
sections.html: Our shop is 45 minutes down Highway 34 through the Big Thompson Canyon, which is close enough to inspect quickly and far enough that we stage mountain jobs properly: materials delivered once, a crew in the valley for the duration, and a weather window planned around the wind forecast rather than the calendar. Every job starts with a free photo-documented roof inspection and a written itemized estimate that spells out the Class A assembly, the snow retention layout, and the ember-resistant details. Call (970) 430-5884 or book an inspection.

faq.q: Can I put a cedar shake roof on my Estes Park home?
faq.a: Natural cedar shake does not meet the Class A requirement that Larimer County applies across the mountain area or the Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code that the town and county have enforced since July 2026 on reroofs replacing 25 percent or more of the covering. Class A synthetic shake keeps the look, resists embers and hail, and satisfies both the code and any HOA covenant, which state law prevents from requiring wood.

faq.q: What snow load does an Estes Park roof have to carry?
faq.a: Under the Larimer County 2024 building code amendments, the minimum design snow load between 7,001 and 8,000 feet is 70 pounds per square foot, and structures above 8,000 feet require engineered design. On a reroof we check the existing framing against that number, replace damaged sheathing, and on metal roofs lay out snow retention on a drawing so sliding snow does not land on a deck, a walkway, or a propane tank.

faq.q: Do you serve Glen Haven, Drake, and the Big Thompson Canyon?
faq.a: Yes. Glen Haven, Drake, Allenspark, Pinewood Springs, and the canyon addresses between Loveland and Estes Park are all in our regular range, and we pass through the canyon on every trip up. Those addresses are permitted through the Larimer County Building Division rather than the town, with the county Class A, Class 4, ice barrier, high-wind attachment, and roofing certification requirements. We confirm jurisdiction before quoting.

faq.q: Does an Estes Park reroof need a permit and inspection?
faq.a: Yes. Inside town limits the permit comes from the Town of Estes Park Community Development department through its Building Safety division, and inspections are requested through the town portal. Outside town limits it is Larimer County. Either way the roof closes on a final inspection, and under the state wildfire code the reviewer will look at the Class A assembly, vent mesh, and noncombustible gutters, not only the covering.

faq.q: Is hail a problem in Estes Park?
faq.a: Less than on the plains, but it is not zero. The National Weather Service logged 1.75 inch hail in Estes Park on July 12, 2007, and smaller hail is common in afternoon summer storms. Larimer County still requires Class 4 asphalt shingles on replacement roofs, and the metal and synthetic systems we recommend for wind and fire carry a Class 4 impact rating anyway, so the hail question is answered by the same roof.

name: Nederland
permitAuthority: Town of Nederland Planning and Zoning Department (plan review and inspections by contract)
title: Nederland Roofing Contractor
description: Nederland roofing contractor for Class A metal, synthetic shake, and ember-resistant re-roofs at 8,236 feet in Boulder County. Get a free inspection.
lede: Nederland sits at 8,236 feet on the Peak to Peak Highway, inside one of the most fire-conscious counties in Colorado. Roofs here are judged by embers, wind, and snow before anything else, and we build them that way.
summary: Class A metal and synthetic roofing for Nederland and the Peak to Peak corridor, built for ember exposure, wind, and 8,000-foot winters.

sections.h2: Roofing in Nederland at 8,236 feet
sections.html:
Nederland is a mining town that became a mountain town, and the roofs show it. Around downtown and Barker Reservoir you find older frame houses and cabins with low-pitched gables, many re-roofed two or three times with asphalt shingles. Up the side roads toward Eldora, Big Springs, and the Caribou area the housing stock shifts to 1970s and later homes on timbered lots, with a mix of metal, shingle, and the occasional aging cedar shake that should have been replaced years ago. Nearly all of it sits in Boulder County's western wildfire zone.

At this elevation the sun does real damage. Ultraviolet exposure is far stronger than it is in Boulder, which is why we see 25-year shingles going brittle in 15. Pair that with a long freeze and thaw season and a roof that was marginal when it went on becomes a leak search by year twelve. Our free photo-documented inspections start with the underlayment and flashing, because that is where Nederland roofs actually fail.

sections.h2: Wildfire interface and ember-resistant roofing
sections.html:
Nederland has watched fire come close more than once. The Cold Springs Fire in July 2016 burned a little over 500 acres about two miles northeast of town and destroyed eight homes near the Peak to Peak Highway and Cold Springs Road. In October 2025 a structure fire destroyed the Caribou Village Shopping Center. Those events are why wildfire is the first conversation we have on any Nederland roof.

The roof is the largest ember catcher on a house. In a wind-driven fire, embers land on the covering, pile up in valleys and against chimneys, and work into attic vents. Boulder County's ignition-resistant construction rules for the unincorporated western county require Class A roof assemblies tested to ASTM E108 or UL 790, metal valley flashing over a 36-inch underlayment, noncombustible gutters, metal drip edge so no sheathing is exposed, and attic vents that are either ember-rated or screened with 1/8-inch noncombustible mesh. The 2025 Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code pushes the same standard across mapped wildland-urban interface areas statewide, and replacing 25 percent or more of a roof covering triggers full compliance.

Natural cedar shake has no place on a Nederland roof. The honest replacements are standing seam metal, stone-coated steel, and Class A synthetic shake that keeps the look without the fuel. Our guide to the best roofing materials for Colorado wildfire zones walks through the tradeoffs.

sections.h2: Snow, wind, and ice dams on the Peak to Peak
sections.html:
Nederland gets upslope storms that dump heavy, wet spring snow, and it gets the Front Range chinook winds that strip whatever is not fastened down. We specify mechanically seamed standing seam metal with clip spacing set for the exposure, and we run full-coverage self-adhered ice and water shield rather than the two-foot minimum. On the north-facing eaves above Middle Boulder Creek, ice dams are routine. Fixing them starts in the attic with air sealing and balanced ventilation, not with heat cable.

Hail is less frequent in Nederland than it is on the plains east of Boulder, and it tends to run smaller, but summer thunderstorms that build over the Divide do drop hail on the town. A Class 4 impact-rated covering costs little extra and pays for itself in insurance conversations.

sections.h2: Permits, HOA approvals, and what the inspector checks
sections.html:
Inside town limits, a re-roof permit goes through the Town of Nederland Planning and Zoning Department, which contracts plan review and inspections to a third-party building services firm. The town requires a wildfire mitigation form that is routed to the Nederland Fire Protection District, so defensible space gets looked at alongside the roof. Addresses outside town limits, which includes most of the Eldora, Magnolia, and Sugarloaf roads, are permitted by Boulder County Community Planning and Permitting under its wildfire zone rules. We confirm which jurisdiction you are in before we write the estimate.

Several subdivisions off the Peak to Peak carry HOA covenants on roof color and material. Where an HOA or design committee is involved we prepare the color chip and product data submittal as part of the job. See how to read a roofing estimate for what the written scope should include.

sections.h2: Serving Nederland from Loveland
sections.html: We reach Nederland from Loveland in about an hour and a half, either down through Boulder and up Boulder Canyon on Highway 119, or along the Peak to Peak from Lyons through Ward. Inspections and repairs are scheduled in the same week on either route. A full roof replacement is staged with materials delivered to the site and a crew that stays through the tear-off and dry-in, because a mountain roof should never be left open overnight. Our building season above 8,000 feet runs roughly May through October, so we book replacements early. Start with a free inspection and we will tell you honestly whether the roof needs work this year or can wait.

faq.q: Is a Class A roof required in Nederland?
faq.a: For addresses in unincorporated Boulder County west of town, yes: the county requires Class A roof assemblies, metal valley flashing, noncombustible gutters, and ember-resistant vents. Inside the town limits the Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code now sets the same floor in mapped wildland-urban interface areas, and replacing a quarter or more of the covering triggers it. We check the map for your parcel before quoting.

faq.q: Can I keep my cedar shake roof in Nederland?
faq.a: You can repair small sections of an existing shake roof, but once a repair reaches 25 percent of the covering the whole roof has to come up to a Class A standard. We would not recommend new wood shake anywhere on the Peak to Peak. Synthetic shake gives the same profile with a Class A rating and far less maintenance.

faq.q: Do you handle the Nederland permit and wildfire form?
faq.a: Yes. We pull the re-roof permit through the Town of Nederland or Boulder County depending on your address, complete the wildfire mitigation form that the fire district reviews, and schedule the inspections. You get copies of everything for your records and your insurer.

faq.q: How long does a metal roof last at 8,236 feet?
faq.a: A properly detailed standing seam roof with a PVDF finish typically runs 40 to 70 years in Colorado. Lifespan varies by exposure, attachment, and ventilation. Our post on how long a roof lasts in Colorado covers what shortens or extends that range at altitude.

name: Winter Park
permitAuthority: Town of Winter Park Building Division
title: Winter Park Roofing Contractor
description: Winter Park roofing contractor for standing seam metal, snow retention, and ice dam fixes at 9,052 feet in Grand County. Get a free inspection.
keywords: ice dam repair winter park co
lede: Winter Park averages more than 200 inches of snow a year and stays frozen for half of it. A roof here is a snow management system first and a weather barrier second.
summary: Standing seam metal, engineered snow retention, and cold-roof ventilation for Winter Park and the Fraser Valley, where winter lasts six months.

sections.h2: What 214 inches of snow does to a Winter Park roof
sections.html:
Winter Park sits at about 9,052 feet at the base of Berthoud Pass, and the Fraser Valley is one of the coldest inhabited places in the lower 48. The town averages roughly 214 inches of snowfall and stays snow-covered for about six months. That changes the math on every roof decision. A snowpack that never melts between storms builds weight, slides without warning, and feeds ice dams every time the sun hits a south face in February.

The housing stock tells the story. Older A-frames and chalets from the 1960s and 1970s line the Vasquez Road and Old Town areas, often with steep metal roofs that shed snow straight onto decks and entries. The newer condo and townhome stock around the resort base, Rendezvous, and the Hideaway area runs to standing seam over complex rooflines with dormers, valleys, and intersecting pitches that trap snow. A large share of these are short-term rentals with owners on the Front Range or out of state, which is why every inspection we do in Winter Park comes back as a photo report you can read from anywhere.

sections.h2: Snow load, sliding snow, and ice dams here
sections.html:
Grand County publishes ground snow loads that climb steeply with elevation, and the Winter Park area is near the top of that table. Structural capacity is a framing question, but the roof covering decides where the snow goes. On metal roofs we lay out snow retention from the manufacturer's engineered calculator based on pitch, panel profile, and the roof snow load, and we put fences or guards above every walkway, deck, meter, and door. Uncontrolled sliding snow off a 10:12 metal roof has crushed railings and cars in this town, and a roof that dumps onto the neighbor's property is a code problem as well as a liability.

Ice dams form when the attic runs warm and the eave stays cold. Heat cable is a bandage. The fix is a cold roof: air sealing at the ceiling, insulation that does not get crushed at the eave, continuous intake and exhaust ventilation, and full-coverage high-temperature ice and water shield under metal. Our article on roofing a mountain home above 8,000 feet explains the assembly in detail.

Wind matters too. Berthoud Pass and the upper valley funnel westerly gusts that peel poorly clipped panels and lift ridge caps. We mechanically seam standing seam panels and set clip spacing for the exposure rather than the catalog default. Hail is uncommon at this elevation compared to the Front Range, but summer cells do drop small hail on the valley and we still recommend impact-rated coverings for any shingle roof.

sections.h2: Wildfire and the 2020 East Troublesome Fire
sections.html: The East Troublesome Fire in October 2020 burned more than 190,000 acres in Grand County and destroyed 555 structures, most of them north of Winter Park toward Granby and Grand Lake. Winter Park was spared, but the beetle-killed lodgepole on the surrounding slopes has not gone anywhere. Under the 2025 Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code, parcels mapped in the wildland-urban interface need a Class A roof covering or assembly, metal valley flashing, and ember-resistant venting, and replacing 25 percent or more of the roof triggers the upgrade. Standing seam metal and Class A synthetic shake both satisfy it and both handle the snow.

sections.h2: What roof systems work in Winter Park
sections.html: Standing seam metal is the default here for good reason: it sheds snow on steep pitches, holds snow on moderate pitches when fitted with retention, carries a Class A rating, and lasts 40 to 70 years. Stone-coated steel suits HOAs that want a shingle profile. Class A synthetic slate and shake fit the alpine look on custom homes. Asphalt shingles are allowed and common on older homes, but at 9,000 feet the UV and freeze cycling shorten their life, and we are candid about that in the estimate. Compare the numbers in our 30-year metal versus asphalt cost comparison.

sections.h2: Permits, HOA review, and scheduling
sections.html:
Re-roofs inside town limits are permitted and inspected by the Town of Winter Park Building Division. Fraser, which shares the valley, has its own process, and county roads outside both towns go through Grand County. Most condo and townhome associations in Winter Park require written approval of roof color and material before a permit is pulled, and some resort-area HOAs restrict work hours and staging locations during ski season. We prepare the HOA submittal with product data and color samples and build the staging plan around it.

The building season is short. Reliable roofing weather runs from late May into October, and the best slots fill by spring. We drive US 40 over Berthoud Pass from Loveland in roughly two hours, stage materials on site, and keep a crew through dry-in so the roof is never open overnight. For a replacement, leak repair, or a pre-sale inspection, start with a free inspection.

faq.q: Do I need snow guards on a metal roof in Winter Park?
faq.a: On almost every metal roof here, yes. Anywhere the eave sits above a deck, walkway, entry, utility meter, or a neighboring lot, retention is the responsible choice and often a code expectation. We size and lay out guards from the manufacturer calculator using the roof snow load and pitch, and we show the layout on a drawing before installing.

faq.q: Why do my gutters fill with ice every winter?
faq.a: Because warm attic air is melting the snowpack from below and the meltwater refreezes at the cold eave. Gutters make the dam worse by holding the ice. The lasting fix is air sealing, proper insulation, and balanced ventilation to keep the roof deck cold, with a high-temperature ice and water membrane as a backstop.

faq.q: Can you work on my rental while I am out of state?
faq.a: Yes. Most of our Winter Park clients are remote owners. We coordinate with your property manager for access, send a photo-documented inspection and written itemized estimate by email, and deliver before, during, and after photos on completion. Nothing proceeds without your written approval.

faq.q: Is hail a concern in Winter Park?
faq.a: Less than it is in Loveland or Greeley, but not zero. Summer thunderstorms over the valley occasionally drop small hail, and a brittle, UV-aged shingle roof can bruise from it. We recommend Class 4 impact-rated shingles if you stay with asphalt, or metal, which shrugs off the small hail typical at this elevation.

name: Granby
permitAuthority: Town of Granby Building Department
title: Granby Roofing Contractor
description: Granby roofing contractor for Class A metal and synthetic roofs, fire rebuilds, and ranch buildings at 7,935 feet in Grand County. Get a free inspection.
lede: Granby is a ranching and lake town at 7,935 feet that learned the hard way in 2020 what a wind-driven fire does to a subdivision. The roofs going on now are built with that memory.
summary: Fire-rated metal and synthetic roofing, snow-ready details, and ranch and outbuilding work for Granby, Lake Granby, and the Fraser River valley.

sections.h2: Granby roofs: ranch country meeting resort country
sections.html:
Granby is where US 40 flattens out between Berthoud Pass and the Colorado River headwaters. At 7,935 feet it is lower and a little drier than Winter Park, with a wider valley, more wind, and a very different mix of buildings. Downtown along Agate Avenue you find early twentieth century frame storefronts and houses, many with low-slope roofs and asphalt shingles that have been layered or patched. Out toward Lake Granby and the Granby Ranch area the stock turns to 1990s and newer homes, log and timber accents, and standing seam metal. On the ranch roads, roofing means barns, shops, and hay sheds with exposed-fastener metal panels that are due for screw replacement or a full re-skin.

Grand County is a different roofing environment from the Front Range. Snow loads are high, UV at nearly 8,000 feet cooks asphalt and fastener washers, and the valley wind finds every loose panel. Hail is less common here than east of the Divide, though summer storms do drop it, and we still write Class 4 impact ratings into shingle estimates for that reason and for the insurance discount.

sections.h2: The East Troublesome Fire and ember-resistant roofs
sections.html:
On October 21 and 22, 2020, the East Troublesome Fire ran more than 100,000 acres in a single night on wind, pushed from the Troublesome Creek drainage east across County Road 125 and the subdivisions north of Granby toward Grand Lake. The final count was 193,812 acres and 555 structures lost, 366 of them homes. Neighborhoods like those around County Road 4 and the lake took the worst of it. Three years later only a fraction of the destroyed homes had rebuild permits, which tells you how long recovery runs in a county with a short building season.

What survived that night were not lucky houses so much as hardened ones: Class A roofs, metal or screened vents, noncombustible gutters, and defensible space. Every Granby roof we touch is built to that standard whether the parcel is mapped as high hazard or not. That means a Class A covering or assembly, metal valley flashing over a cap sheet, drip edge covering all sheathing, ember-resistant attic ventilation, and no wood shake anywhere. The 2025 Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code now requires this in mapped wildland-urban interface areas statewide and triggers it when a quarter or more of the roof is replaced. Our guide to the best roofing materials for Colorado wildfire zones compares metal, stone-coated steel, and Class A synthetic shake for homes that want the mountain look.

sections.h2: Snow load, ice, and wind in the Fraser River valley
sections.html:
Granby's snow is lighter than Winter Park's but it stays on the roof for months, and the valley sees sustained west and southwest wind that drifts snow against dormers and parapets. Drift load on a low-slope section next to a taller wall can exceed the uniform load by a wide margin, and that is where we see sagging decks and separated seams on older commercial buildings downtown. On homes, the common failure is ice damming at north eaves where the attic runs warm. We treat that with air sealing and ventilation first and full-coverage ice and water shield under the covering.

On standing seam metal we lay out snow retention from the manufacturer's engineered calculator and place it above every door, deck, walkway, propane tank, and meter. We mechanically seam panels and tighten clip spacing on exposed ridgeline lots. For ranch buildings we re-skin with heavier gauge panels and replace every fastener rather than chasing individual leaks.

sections.h2: Permits in Granby and the surrounding county
sections.html:
Granby runs its own building department now. The Town of Granby Building Department adopted the 2021 International Codes with local amendments and takes permit applications through an online portal; through early 2026 it used a neighboring town's building division during the transition. If your address is outside town limits, which includes most of the lake and ranch properties, the permit goes through the Grand County Building Department instead. We confirm jurisdiction with the town zoning map before we write the estimate so the permit does not stall the start date.

Granby Ranch and the lakeside subdivisions have HOA covenants on roof color and reflectivity, and several require a design review approval before the town will issue a permit. We prepare that submittal with product data and color chips. On a fire rebuild, we also coordinate with your insurer's scope, and we never pay or waive a deductible, which Colorado law prohibits. See our insurance claim roofing page for how that process works.

sections.h2: Getting to Granby from Loveland
sections.html: Granby is a little over two hours from our Loveland office by I-70 and US 40 over Berthoud Pass, or by US 34 over Trail Ridge Road when it is open in summer. We group Grand County inspections so a drive serves several homes, and we stage full replacements with on-site material delivery and a crew that stays through dry-in. The practical building season here runs late May to mid-October. Book a free inspection early in the year if you want a replacement done before the snow flies.

faq.q: Who issues roof permits in Granby?
faq.a: Inside town limits, the Town of Granby Building Department, which operates under the 2021 International Codes with local amendments. Properties outside town limits, including most lakeside and ranch parcels, are permitted and inspected by the Grand County Building Department. We confirm your jurisdiction from the town zoning map before quoting and pull the permit ourselves.

faq.q: What roof should I put on a home rebuilt after the East Troublesome Fire?
faq.a: A Class A assembly with no gaps for embers: standing seam metal or Class A synthetic shake over a cap sheet or self-adhered membrane, metal valleys, metal drip edge, noncombustible gutters, and ember-rated vents. Match it with defensible space. That combination is what the surviving houses in the burn area had in common.

faq.q: Can you re-roof a barn or shop on a Granby ranch?
faq.a: Yes. Agricultural metal re-skins are common work for us in Grand County. We replace every fastener, upgrade to heavier gauge panels where the purlins allow, add closure strips at eaves and ridges to stop wind-driven snow, and set snow retention above doors and feed areas. Written itemized estimates cover the whole building, not just the leaking bay.

faq.q: Does Granby get hail?
faq.a: Occasionally, and usually small. Granby is west of the Front Range hail belt, so damaging hail is far rarer than in Loveland or Greeley, but summer storms do drop pea to marble hail on the valley. We still specify Class 4 impact-rated shingles when a shingle roof is chosen, because the rating also helps with insurance.

name: Grand Lake
permitAuthority: Town of Grand Lake (permits and inspections through the Grand County Building Department)
title: Grand Lake Roofing Contractor
description: Grand Lake roofing contractor for fire-rated metal and synthetic roofs, cabin re-roofs, and snow retention at 8,369 feet. Get a free inspection.
keywords: cabin roof replacement grand lake colorado
lede: Grand Lake lost a large share of its surrounding homes to the East Troublesome Fire in October 2020. Roofing here now means Class A assemblies, ember-tight details, and respect for a village that still looks like 1920.
summary: Ember-resistant Class A roofing for Grand Lake cabins, lakefront homes, and rebuilds at the west entrance to Rocky Mountain National Park.

sections.h2: Roofing the village at the headwaters
sections.html:
Grand Lake sits at 8,369 feet at the west gate of Rocky Mountain National Park, on the shore of the state's largest natural lake, with a boardwalk main street of log and false-front buildings and a year-round population of a few hundred. The surrounding lots hold a century of cabin architecture: 1920s and 1930s log cabins with steep shingle or rolled roofs, mid-century lake cottages, and a newer ring of timber-frame homes and short-term rentals along the lake and up the hillsides toward Columbine Lake and the Shadow Mountain Reservoir shore. Many owners are seasonal and live on the Front Range, in Texas, or farther, which is why we document everything in photos and deliver estimates by email.

The roofing challenges are the same three that govern every Grand County town, in a sharper form: snow that stays for six months, intense ultraviolet exposure, and wildfire. Hail is rare at this elevation and usually small, though a July storm can still bruise a sun-aged shingle roof. What really ages a Grand Lake roof is the sun and the freeze cycle, and what really threatens it is fire.

sections.h2: After East Troublesome: ember-resistant roofing by default
sections.html:
On the night of October 21, 2020, the East Troublesome Fire crossed County Road 125 and ran into the Grand Lake area on 60-mile-per-hour wind, then jumped the Continental Divide the next day. It burned 193,812 acres before containment on November 30 and destroyed 555 structures, 366 of them homes, with the heaviest losses in the subdivisions around Grand Lake and north of Granby. Two residents who stayed in their home outside town died.

The rebuilds and the surviving homes share a lesson. Embers, not flame fronts, ignite most houses, and the roof catches the most embers. Our Grand Lake roofs are built to the ignition-resistant standard whether or not a parcel is mapped as high hazard under the 2025 Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code: a Class A covering or assembly, firestopping or a cap sheet under any covering that creates a space over the deck, metal valley flashing over a 36-inch cap sheet, metal drip edge so no sheathing shows, noncombustible gutters, and attic vents that are ember-rated or screened with 1/8-inch noncombustible mesh. Replacing 25 percent or more of a roof covering triggers the full standard. The materials guide for Colorado wildfire zones lays out the options; for Grand Lake that usually means standing seam metal on new and timber-frame homes and Class A synthetic shake on cabins where the owner or the town's character review wants the historic texture.

sections.h2: Snow load, sliding snow, and ice on the lake
sections.html: Grand Lake's snow is deep and persistent. Grand County sets ground snow loads by elevation, and at 8,369 feet the design numbers are high enough that older cabin rafters deserve a look before a heavier covering goes on. On steep metal roofs the question is not whether the snow comes off but where it lands. We lay out snow retention from the manufacturer's engineered calculator and protect every door, deck, walkway, and propane tank. On cabins with low attic space, ice dams at the eaves are chronic; we address them with air sealing and ventilation first, then full-coverage high-temperature ice and water shield beneath the covering. Our article on snow load and ice dams above 8,000 feet explains the assembly.

sections.h2: Permits, the Grand County inspector, and HOA review
sections.html: The Town of Grand Lake directs all building permits and all inspections through the Grand County Building Department, which handles applications online, while the town itself reviews zoning and requires a material and color sample for the roof as part of the submittal. Properties outside town limits on the lake and reservoir shores go straight to the county. Several lakeside subdivisions and the newer timber-frame developments carry HOA covenants on roof color, reflectivity, and material; we prepare that submittal with product data and chips. On a fire-related or storm claim we work from the insurer's scope and never pay or waive a deductible, which Colorado law prohibits.

sections.h2: Serving Grand Lake from Loveland
sections.html: In summer the drive from Loveland is the scenic one: US 34 through Estes Park and over Trail Ridge Road, about two and a half hours. When Trail Ridge closes for the season we come around by I-70 and US 40 through Granby, closer to three hours. Either way, we group Grand County inspections together and stage full replacements with on-site delivery and a crew that stays through dry-in. The working season at this elevation is roughly late May through early October, so a replacement should be booked by spring. A free photo-documented inspection is the place to start.

faq.q: What roof is best for a Grand Lake cabin?
faq.a: Class A synthetic shake if you want to keep the historic look, or standing seam metal if you want the longest life and the best snow shedding. Both are Class A. On a 1920s cabin we also check rafter capacity before adding weight and address ventilation so ice dams do not come back with the new roof.

faq.q: Who inspects a roof permit in Grand Lake?
faq.a: The Grand County Building Department. The Town of Grand Lake routes all building permits and inspections to the county, while the town reviews zoning and asks for a roof material and color sample. Properties outside the town limits on the lake and reservoir go directly to the county. We handle the application and the inspections.

faq.q: Are wood shake roofs allowed in Grand Lake?
faq.a: A wood shake roof can be patched in small amounts, but once repairs reach 25 percent of the covering the entire roof must meet the Class A standard under the Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code in mapped interface areas. After the East Troublesome Fire we would not install new wood shake anywhere in the Grand Lake area under any circumstances.

faq.q: How does hail factor into a Grand Lake roof?
faq.a: Hail is rare and typically small here compared to the Front Range, so it is not the main driver of roof wear. Sun, freeze cycling, snow weight, and fire are. That said, a sun-aged shingle roof can bruise from a summer storm, and impact-rated coverings cost little more. We note hail risk honestly in every inspection report.

name: Steamboat Springs
permitAuthority: Routt County Regional Building Department (serving the City of Steamboat Springs)
title: Steamboat Springs Roofing
description: Steamboat Springs roofing contractor for heavy-snow metal roofs, ice dam fixes, and Class A re-roofs at 6,695 feet in Routt County. Get a free inspection.
lede: Steamboat Springs gets some of the deepest, wettest snow in Colorado and the ice dams to match. Roofing here is a structural and thermal problem that happens to keep the rain out.
summary: Heavy-snow standing seam metal, engineered snow retention, ice dam elimination, and Class A re-roofs for Steamboat Springs and the Yampa Valley.

sections.h2: Snow country roofing at 6,695 feet
sections.html:
Steamboat is lower than the Summit County towns, at about 6,695 feet downtown, but it sits in the path of northwest storm flow that stacks snow on the Yampa Valley all winter. The ski mountain regularly passes 300 inches and topped 400 inches at mid-mountain in the 2022 to 2023 season. Town gets less, but it is the heavy, settling kind that compacts into a dense load by February. The Routt County Regional Building Department amendments put the ground snow load in the Steamboat area above 100 pounds per square foot, and roof design loads in the 75 pound range are typical on new work.

The housing stock spans Old Town's Victorian and early 1900s miner and rancher houses with steep gables, the 1970s and 1980s condominium stock along the mountain base and Walton Creek, and newer custom and timber homes in the Fish Creek, Sanctuary, and Elk River areas. Standing seam metal dominates the newer work. A lot of the condo stock still carries aging asphalt shingle under decades of ice dam scarring.

sections.h2: Ice dams, snow retention, and the 2011 windstorm
sections.html:
Steamboat's ice dams are legendary for a reason. Deep snow insulates the roof, interior heat melts the bottom of the pack, and meltwater refreezes at the eave into dams that back water under shingles and into walls. Heat cable is a seasonal patch. The fix is a cold roof: air sealing and insulation at the ceiling plane, continuous ventilation from eave to ridge, and full-coverage high-temperature ice and water membrane under metal. On complex roofs with dormers and valleys we sometimes add a vented over-roof. Our guide to snow load and ice dams on mountain homes explains each piece.

Sliding snow is the other hazard. A standing seam roof that releases a winter's load in one slab can take out a deck rail, a gas meter, or a person. We lay out snow retention from the manufacturer's engineered calculator using the actual roof snow load and pitch, and we protect every entry, walkway, and meter. Wind is not a daily problem the way it is in Estes Park, but on December 1, 2011, gusts reached 123 miles per hour on the ski area peaks and tore roofs and windows off condominiums at the base, a reminder that mechanical seaming and proper clip spacing are not optional.

Hail is infrequent in the Yampa Valley compared to the Front Range, but summer storms do produce it. We still recommend Class 4 impact-rated shingles where asphalt is chosen, partly for the insurance credit.

sections.h2: Wildfire code: Routt County went to Class A
sections.html: Routt County and its municipalities adopted sections of the International Wildland-Urban Interface Code countywide, moving the roof standard from Class B to Class A, requiring noncombustible gutters and downspouts, and screening roof, wall, and soffit vents with noncombustible mesh. The statewide 2025 Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code layers on top for mapped interface parcels and treats replacing 25 percent or more of a roof as a full upgrade trigger. The hillsides above town are classic interface ground. Metal, stone-coated steel, and Class A synthetic shake all qualify; natural cedar shake does not, and we do not install it here. Our wildfire zone materials guide compares the options.

sections.h2: Permits, inspections, and HOA review in Steamboat
sections.html:
The Routt County Regional Building Department administers building permits and inspections for the City of Steamboat Springs as well as unincorporated Routt County, so a re-roof permit for a house on Oak Street and a cabin up the Elk River both go through the same office in the downtown courthouse annex. The inspector will want to see underlayment, valley metal, and drip edge before the covering goes down, and the final after cleanup.

Most of the mountain-base condominium and townhome associations have HOA rules on roof color, material, and work windows during ski season, and some require a board vote before a permit is pulled. We prepare the HOA submittal with product data and color samples. For remote owners of short-term rentals, every inspection comes back as a photo report with a written itemized estimate, and we send completion photos before you ever see the roof in person.

sections.h2: Serving Steamboat Springs from Loveland
sections.html: Steamboat is our longest regular drive, a little over three hours by I-70 and Colorado 9 through Kremmling or by US 40 over Rabbit Ears Pass. We do not pretend otherwise. We make it work by bundling inspections, staging full replacements with on-site delivery, and keeping a crew in town through dry-in rather than commuting. The season runs roughly May through October and books up early. If you are weighing a replacement or need a pre-listing inspection, start with a free inspection and we will be straightforward about timing.

faq.q: Can a metal roof stop ice dams in Steamboat?
faq.a: A metal roof sheds meltwater better than shingles and does not absorb it, but it will not stop a dam on its own if the attic runs warm. Ice dams are a heat problem. We pair metal with air sealing, insulation, balanced ventilation, and full-coverage high-temperature membrane. Done together, that combination ends chronic damming on most Steamboat homes.

faq.q: Who issues roof permits in Steamboat Springs?
faq.a: The Routt County Regional Building Department, which handles permits and inspections for the city and unincorporated county from its office in the downtown courthouse annex. We pull the permit, schedule the underlayment and final inspections, and provide copies of everything to you and, if needed, your HOA or insurer.

faq.q: Is Class A roofing required in Steamboat?
faq.a: Yes. Routt County adopted wildland-urban interface code sections countywide that raised the roof standard to Class A along with noncombustible gutters and screened vents, and the statewide Wildfire Resiliency Code applies in mapped interface areas. Metal, impact-rated shingles, stone-coated steel, and synthetic shake all meet it. Wood shake does not.

faq.q: Do you really travel to Steamboat from Loveland?
faq.a: Yes, for jobs that justify mobilizing a crew: full replacements, multi-unit and HOA re-roofs, and custom homes. We stage materials in town and keep the crew there through dry-in. For a single small repair we will tell you honestly whether the trip makes sense or whether a local handyman is the better call.

name: Breckenridge
permitAuthority: Town of Breckenridge Community Development (Building Department and Planning Department)
title: Breckenridge Roofing Contractor
description: Breckenridge roofing contractor for Class A metal and synthetic roofs, historic district re-roofs, and snow retention at 9,600 feet. Get a free inspection.
lede: At 9,600 feet with a Victorian historic district, a design code that reviews roof color, and 90 to 100 pound snow loads, Breckenridge is the most paperwork-intensive roof in Colorado. We treat it like the construction project it is.
summary: Design-code-compliant Class A roofing, full ice and water coverage, and engineered snow retention for Breckenridge homes, condos, and the historic district.

sections.h2: Breckenridge roofs: 1880s storefronts to 9,600-foot ski-in homes
sections.html:
Breckenridge has one of the largest historic districts in Colorado, a core of 1880s and 1890s clapboard and log buildings along Main Street and the side streets east of the Blue River, and then rings of 1970s condominiums at the base of Peak 8 and Peak 9, 1990s townhomes in Warriors Mark and Wellington, and large timber homes on the hillsides in the Highlands and up Boreas Pass Road. The town averages about 185 inches of snow and sits at roughly 9,600 feet, which means a six-month roof load and the harshest ultraviolet exposure of any town we serve. Hail is infrequent at this elevation and usually small, but the sun does in ten years what Loveland's hail does in one.

A large share of the housing stock is short-term rental with owners who live elsewhere. Our Breckenridge inspections come back as photo reports with written itemized estimates, and we send completion photos before you see the roof. On a Summit County HOA re-roof we manage the whole thing as a project: schedule, staging, crane logistics, safety plan, and submittals.

sections.h2: What the Town of Breckenridge requires on a re-roof
sections.html:
The Town of Breckenridge Building Department is specific about roofs, and we build to its handout. Every roof covering on new construction, additions, and re-roofs must be Class A. The town requires full-coverage self-adhered polymer-modified bitumen underlayment, the product most people call ice and water shield, across the entire roof, not just the eaves. Under any metal roofing it must be the high-temperature version. At the underlayment inspection the inspector verifies complete coverage, valley metal, and drip edge before any covering goes down, and the final inspection comes after the site is clean. We schedule both and are on the roof for both.

Summit County's design matrix puts roof snow loads in the Breckenridge area at 90 to 100 pounds per square foot, with 115 mile per hour design wind and 40-inch frost depth. Soffit and gable vents are limited to 3/16-inch openings as a wildfire measure, which is stricter than the 1/4-inch mesh in some neighboring jurisdictions. For how these numbers shape the assembly, read roofing a mountain home above 8,000 feet.

sections.h2: Design review, the historic district, and HOA approvals
sections.html:
Roofing in Breckenridge is also a planning question. The Development Code's architectural compatibility policy expects roof materials to be nonreflective and to blend into the site's backdrop, and it lists reflective metal roofing among inappropriate materials. In practice that means low-gloss, darker standing seam finishes and matte synthetic profiles. Inside the Local Historic District, the Handbook of Design Standards for the Historic and Conservation Districts governs, and a re-roof on a contributing structure may need the Planning Department to approve the material, profile, and color before a building permit issues. We prepare those submittals with product data and chips and have sat through enough hearings to know what passes.

Nearly every condo and townhome in town has an HOA with its own roof standards and ski-season work restrictions, and the resort-adjacent associations often limit staging and crane use to shoulder season. We build the schedule around those rules rather than fighting them.

sections.h2: Wildfire and the roof systems that fit Breckenridge
sections.html:
Summit County's lodgepole forests were hit hard by beetle kill, and the town has long required Class A roofs and ember-resistant venting as a result. The 2025 Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code applies in mapped wildland-urban interface parcels and makes replacing 25 percent or more of a roof covering a full-upgrade trigger. Natural wood shake, once common on 1970s Breckenridge chalets, is not a Class A covering and should not go back on.

The systems that satisfy the building department, the design code, and the snow all at once are mechanically seamed standing seam metal in a low-gloss finish with engineered snow retention, Class A synthetic shake or slate on homes that want the historic texture, and Class 4 impact-rated shingles where an HOA requires a shingle profile and the budget calls for it. Snow retention goes above every entry, deck, walkway, and meter, laid out from the manufacturer's calculator using the actual roof snow load. Our 30-year cost comparison shows why metal usually wins at this elevation.

sections.h2: Serving Breckenridge from Loveland
sections.html: Breckenridge is a little over two hours from Loveland by I-70 and Colorado 9 through Frisco. For a full roof replacement or HOA project we stage materials on site, arrange crane lifts where the lot demands it, and keep the crew in Summit County through dry-in so the roof is never open overnight. The practical season at 9,600 feet is June through early October, and the design review and HOA steps add weeks on the front end, so a spring start on paperwork matters. Begin with a free inspection and we will map out the approvals and the calendar together.

faq.q: Does Breckenridge require ice and water shield over the whole roof?
faq.a: Yes. The Town of Breckenridge Building Department requires full-coverage self-adhered polymer-modified bitumen underlayment on re-roofs, with the high-temperature version under any metal roofing. The inspector verifies complete coverage along with valley metal and drip edge at the underlayment inspection before the covering goes on.

faq.q: Can I put a bright metal roof on my Breckenridge home?
faq.a: Probably not. The Development Code expects nonreflective roof materials that blend into the backdrop and lists reflective metal roofing as inappropriate. Low-gloss, darker standing seam finishes are routinely approved. Inside the historic district the Handbook of Design Standards adds material and profile rules, and the Planning Department may need to approve before a building permit issues.

faq.q: What snow load is a Breckenridge roof designed for?
faq.a: Summit County’s design matrix lists roof snow loads of 90 to 100 pounds per square foot for Breckenridge-area subdivisions, with 115 mile per hour wind and a 40-inch frost depth. Those numbers govern framing and also drive how we lay out snow retention, since a full winter’s load releasing off a metal roof is a safety issue.

faq.q: Do you work with Breckenridge HOAs and remote owners?
faq.a: Constantly. Most of our Breckenridge work is for owners who live elsewhere and for associations with ski-season restrictions. We prepare HOA and design review submittals, schedule staging and crane work in the shoulder season, send photo-documented inspections and itemized estimates by email, and deliver completion photos before you see the roof in person.

name: Frisco
permitAuthority: Town of Frisco Community Development Department
title: Frisco CO Roofing Contractor
description: Frisco CO roofing contractor for standing seam metal, condo and townhome re-roofs, and Class A wildfire roofing at 9,097 feet. Get a free inspection.
lede: Frisco calls itself the Main Street of the Rockies, and its roofs range from 1880s false fronts to lakeside townhomes at 9,097 feet. All of them carry 80-plus pounds of snow per square foot by February.
summary: Condo, townhome, and single-family re-roofs in Frisco with standing seam metal, engineered snow retention, and Class A wildfire details for Summit County.

sections.h2: Frisco roofs from Main Street to the Dillon Reservoir shore
sections.html:
Frisco sits at 9,097 feet where Tenmile Creek meets Dillon Reservoir, with I-70 on one side and the Tenmile Range on the other. The historic core along Main Street keeps a handful of 1880s frame buildings, but the bulk of the housing is 1970s through 1990s condominiums and townhomes in the Bills Ranch, Lagoon, and Water Dance areas, plus newer single-family homes and duplexes on the hillside streets north of Main. Much of it is second-home and short-term rental stock, which means remote owners, HOA boards, and property managers are usually who we are talking to.

Condo roofs here fail in predictable ways: shingle roofs installed in the 1990s that have baked under 9,000-foot ultraviolet, metal roofs with original exposed fasteners whose washers gave out, and roof-to-wall intersections where years of ice damming have worked water into the sheathing. Hail is infrequent in Frisco compared to the Front Range and is usually small, so it is rarely the cause of a roof problem; sun, snow, and ice are.

sections.h2: Snow, ice dams, and the Summit County numbers
sections.html:
Summit County's design matrix lists roof snow loads of 80 pounds per square foot for the Frisco Heights and Frisco Terrace subdivisions, with higher values in the zones toward Breckenridge, and a design wind of 115 miles per hour. On a townhome with a long, shared, moderately pitched roof, that load sits for months and slides all at once in a March thaw. We lay out snow retention from the manufacturer's engineered calculator for every metal roof and place it above entries, decks, walkways, parking, and gas meters, because sliding snow onto a neighbor's deck or a parked car is the most common complaint an HOA board brings us.

Ice dams on Frisco condos usually trace to a warm, poorly ventilated attic shared across several units. The fix is air sealing and balanced ventilation at the building level, plus full-coverage high-temperature ice and water shield under the covering. Our article on snow load and ice dams above 8,000 feet walks through the assembly for both single-family homes and multi-unit buildings.

sections.h2: Wildfire interface and Class A coverings
sections.html: Frisco is surrounded by beetle-killed lodgepole in the White River National Forest, and the town is working through adoption of the state's wildland-urban interface requirements under the 2025 Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code, which sets Class A roof coverings or assemblies, metal valley flashing, and ember-resistant vents as the floor in mapped interface areas, with replacement of 25 percent or more of a roof as the upgrade trigger. Summit County's own standard already calls for Class A roofs and vents limited to 3/16-inch openings. We build every Frisco roof to that level regardless of the map. Standing seam metal, stone-coated steel, and Class A synthetic shake all qualify; natural cedar shake, still present on a few 1970s buildings in town, does not and should come off at replacement. See our wildfire zone materials guide for the comparison.

sections.h2: Permits, Rapid Review, and HOA approvals in Frisco
sections.html:
The Town of Frisco Community Development Department permits re-roofs, and a straightforward re-roof qualifies for the town's Rapid Review track through its online permit portal with a stated turnaround of about 72 business hours. Electrical and solar work on the same building goes through the Summit County Building Department. On a multi-unit building the permit is pulled in the association's name and the inspection sequence covers underlayment, valley metal, and drip edge before covering, then a final.

Nearly every Frisco condo and townhome is governed by an HOA with written roof standards on color, material, and profile, and most restrict work and staging during the ski season. We prepare the HOA package with product data and color samples, present at the board meeting if asked, and provide an itemized scope the board can compare line by line. Our guide on how to read a roofing estimate is written for exactly that review.

sections.h2: Serving Frisco from Loveland
sections.html: Frisco is about two hours from Loveland straight down I-70 through the Eisenhower Tunnel, which makes it one of the easier Summit County trips for us. Full replacements and HOA re-roofs are staged with on-site delivery and a crew that stays in the county through dry-in. The working season runs June through early October, and multi-unit projects should have HOA approval in hand by May. Book a free inspection early, or ask us for a reserve study inspection if your board needs a roof condition report for budgeting.

faq.q: Does a re-roof in Frisco need a permit?
faq.a: Yes. The Town of Frisco Community Development Department requires a permit for re-roofing, and standard re-roofs can go through the Rapid Review track in the online portal with a turnaround of roughly 72 business hours. We pull the permit, schedule the underlayment and final inspections, and give the HOA or owner copies of everything.

faq.q: How do you handle a multi-building condo re-roof in Frisco?
faq.a: As a managed project. We provide a roof condition report for the board, an itemized scope per building, an HOA submittal with product data and color samples, a staging and crane plan that respects ski-season restrictions, and a schedule that finishes each building to dry-in before moving on. Owners get photo updates throughout.

faq.q: What is the snow load on a Frisco roof?
faq.a: Summit County lists roof snow loads of 80 pounds per square foot for the Frisco Heights and Frisco Terrace subdivisions, with 115 mile per hour design wind. Other Frisco zones vary. The number matters for framing and for snow retention layout, which we calculate per roof from the manufacturer’s engineered tool rather than guessing.

faq.q: Is hail damage common in Frisco?
faq.a: No. Frisco sits well west of the Front Range hail belt, and the hail that reaches 9,097 feet is usually small. Most roof damage we document here is from ultraviolet aging, ice dams, snow slides, and failed fasteners. If a summer storm does bring hail, we inspect and document it the same way we would in Loveland.

name: Silverthorne
permitAuthority: Town of Silverthorne Community Development Department (plan review and inspections with the Summit County Building Department)
title: Silverthorne Roofing Contractor
description: Silverthorne roofing contractor for metal re-roofs, condo and townhome projects, and Class A wildfire roofing at 8,790 feet. Get a free inspection.
lede: Silverthorne grew from a dam construction camp into the fastest-growing town in Summit County, and its roofs span sixty years of building. At 8,790 feet, all of them answer to the same snow, sun, and fire.
summary: Roof replacement and repair for Silverthorne, Wildernest, and the Blue River valley: standing seam metal, snow retention, and Class A fire-rated systems.

sections.h2: Roofing a town that doubled in a generation
sections.html:
Silverthorne sits at 8,790 feet on the Blue River just below Dillon Dam, with the Gore Range to the west and the Williams Fork and Ptarmigan ranges to the east. The town went from a few hundred people in 1970 to more than 4,000 by 2020, and the roofs mark the eras: 1970s and 1980s condominiums at Wildernest and along Ryan Gulch Road on the steep hillside above town, 1990s townhomes and duplexes near the river, and the newer single-family and multifamily neighborhoods at Angler Mountain Ranch, Summit Sky Ranch, and the Smith Ranch area north along the Blue. Most of the older hillside stock carries asphalt shingles that have cooked under 8,800-foot ultraviolet for far longer than their rating, and a lot of the newer work is standing seam metal.

Hail is uncommon here compared to the Front Range and usually small, so it is rarely what brings a Silverthorne roof down. Sun, freeze cycling, drifting snow on the Wildernest slopes, and ice damming on north eaves are the real wear.

sections.h2: Snow load, drifting, and sliding snow on the hillside
sections.html:
Summit County's design matrix puts roof snow loads around Silverthorne in the 70 to 90 pound per square foot range depending on zone, with a 115 mile per hour design wind and 40-inch frost depth. The Wildernest condominiums are the textbook case for drift: long stepped buildings on a steep west-facing slope where wind off the Gore Range piles snow against upper walls and loads the lower roofs unevenly. On metal, we lay out snow retention from the manufacturer's engineered calculator and protect every stairway, entry, deck, parking area, and meter, because a shed slab off a shared roof is both a safety and an HOA liability issue.

Ice dams on the older stock trace to warm, under-ventilated attics. Our approach is air sealing, insulation that is not crushed at the eave, continuous eave-to-ridge ventilation, and full-coverage high-temperature ice and water membrane under the covering. For the full reasoning, read roofing a mountain home above 8,000 feet.

sections.h2: Wildfire interface and ember-resistant roofing
sections.html: The slopes above Wildernest and up the Blue River are beetle-killed lodgepole and classic wildland-urban interface. Summit County's standard already calls for Class A roofs and soffit and gable vents limited to 3/16-inch openings, and the 2025 Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code applies in mapped interface parcels with Class A coverings or assemblies, metal valley flashing over a cap sheet, and ember-resistant venting, triggered by replacing 25 percent or more of a roof. We build every Silverthorne roof to that standard. Standing seam metal, stone-coated steel, and Class A synthetic shake or slate qualify; wood shake does not and should not go back on. Our guide to roofing materials for Colorado wildfire zones compares them.

sections.h2: Permits and approvals in Silverthorne
sections.html:
The Town of Silverthorne Community Development Department issues building permits and works with the Summit County Building Department on code plan review and field inspections, which are by appointment on weekdays. Silverthorne is unusual in Summit County in that a like-for-like residential re-roof that does not change the roof structure does not require a permit from the town, while a commercial re-roof requires emailing the roof color and material to the Planning Department for approval first. Structural changes, such as adding an over-roof or replacing decking, do require a permit. We confirm the current rule with the department before each job rather than assuming, because towns update these policies. When an inspection is required, the plans, inspection card, and plan notes have to be on site in color or the inspection is not performed.

HOA review is the real gate in Silverthorne. Wildernest, the river townhomes, and the newer master-planned neighborhoods all have written roof standards on color, material, and reflectivity, and many restrict work and staging during ski season. We prepare the HOA submittal with product data and color chips and present at board meetings on request. Our guide to reading a roofing estimate is written for boards comparing bids.

sections.h2: Serving Silverthorne from Loveland
sections.html: Silverthorne is the first Summit County exit off I-70 after the Eisenhower Tunnel, about two hours from Loveland. We bundle Summit County inspections, stage full replacements with on-site delivery and crane lifts where the hillside lots demand it, and keep the crew in the county through dry-in. The working season is June through early October. For remote owners we deliver photo-documented inspections and written itemized estimates by email and completion photos on the last day. Start with a free inspection.

faq.q: Do I need a permit to re-roof my house in Silverthorne?
faq.a: As of the town’s current policy, a like-for-like residential re-roof that does not modify the roof structure does not require a town permit, while commercial re-roofs need Planning Department color and material approval and structural changes need a full permit. We confirm with the Community Development Department before every job because these policies change.

faq.q: What roof works best on a Wildernest condo?
faq.a: Mechanically seamed standing seam metal in a low-gloss finish with engineered snow retention, over full-coverage high-temperature ice and water membrane and a ventilated assembly. The steep west-facing slope drifts heavily and sheds hard, so retention layout and protecting stairways and parking matter as much as the panel choice.

faq.q: How do you handle sliding snow off a metal roof?
faq.a: We size and lay out snow guards or fences from the manufacturer’s engineered calculator using the roof snow load and pitch, then place them above every entry, deck, walkway, parking area, and gas meter. The layout is shown on a drawing before installation. Uncontrolled slides off shared roofs are the most common HOA complaint we are called to fix.

faq.q: Is hail a factor in Silverthorne?
faq.a: Rarely. Silverthorne is west of the Front Range hail belt and the hail that reaches 8,790 feet is usually small. Ultraviolet aging, ice dams, drifted snow, and failed fasteners cause most of the roof damage we document here. We still note hail risk honestly in every inspection report and photograph any impact marks we find.
