sections.h2: Roofing in Vail at 8,150 feet
sections.html: Vail runs eleven miles along Gore Creek and I-70 at about 8,150 feet in Eagle County, from East Vail through the Village and Lionshead to West Vail and Intermountain. The 1960s and 1970s Village and Lionshead core was built to look like a European ski town, with steep gabled roofs, deep overhangs, and heavy timber details. East Vail and the Booth Creek area hold 1970s chalets and townhomes under the Gore Range, while West Vail and the Matterhorn and Intermountain neighborhoods mix 1970s duplexes with large newer custom homes. The town averages about 200 inches of snow and stays below freezing from late fall into spring. Hail is rare and small at this elevation compared with the Front Range; the sun and the snow are what age a Vail roof.

sections.h2: Snow load written into town code
sections.html:
The Town of Vail amends the residential code with its own structural numbers: a ground snow load of 142 pounds per square foot, a roof snow load of 100 pounds per square foot on pitches below 4:12 and 80 pounds on 4:12 and steeper, and the same loads on decks and balconies. The code also requires that new roofs be designed so snow does not slide onto utility meters or neighboring property, with a narrow exception for short overhangs. On standing seam metal that means snow retention laid out from the manufacturer's engineered calculator for the actual roof load and pitch, placed above every entry, deck, walkway, meter, and lot line.

Vail's ice barrier rule is also stricter than the model code. Self-adhered polymer-modified bitumen membrane, or two cemented layers of underlayment, must cover all roof surfaces under shingles, metal panels, and roll roofing, not just the eaves. Under metal we use the high-temperature version. Ice dams on the deep-eaved Village chalets still happen when attics run warm, and we address that with air sealing and balanced ventilation rather than heat cable. Our article on snow load and ice dams above 8,000 feet explains why.

sections.h2: Class A, no wood shake, and ember protection
sections.html: Vail requires every roof assembly or covering in town to be Class A and prohibits wood shakes and shingles outright. Where a covering leaves a space above the deck that could admit flame or embers, that space must be blocked or covered with a cap sheet. A nonconforming roof, which in practice means the old cedar shake still on some 1970s East Vail and West Vail homes, can be repaired once for 25 percent or less of its area; anything larger, or a second repair, means replacing the whole covering. Emergency patches under 10 square feet are exempt, and metal and concrete systems are excepted from the repair cap. The Gore Range and Vail Mountain slopes are wildland-urban interface, and the 2025 Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code reinforces the same Class A and ember-resistant vent standards. For the material choices that satisfy both, see roofing materials for Colorado wildfire zones.

sections.h2: The Design Review Board and what it approves
sections.html:
Every exterior change in Vail, including a re-roof, goes through Design Review under the town's design standards. The roof section lists concrete tile, slate, metal, asphalt and fiberglass shingle, and built-up roofing as materials that may be permitted and prohibits wood shake, wood shingles, and rolled roofing. Metal roofing has to be heavy gauge with visual relief such as a standing seam, must have a low-gloss finish or weather to a dull one, and may not reflect direct sunlight onto adjacent property. Exposed flashing, flues, and rooftop equipment must be painted, anodized, or weather to a nonreflective finish. Rooflines may not deposit snow on parking, trash enclosures, stairways, decks, balconies, or entries, and secondary roofs, snow clips, or snow guards are expected where they would.

The Design Review Board decides whether an unlisted material is acceptable, whether a duplex or multifamily roof may use a different material, and whether a replacement material is compatible with an existing nonconforming roof. We prepare the DRB application with product data, color samples, and the snow retention layout, and we carry the HOA approval for Village, Lionshead, and East Vail associations alongside it. Class A synthetic shake and slate are frequently the answer when an association wants the historic texture that cedar used to provide.

sections.h2: Permits, inspections, and serving Vail from Loveland
sections.html: Once the Design Review approval is in hand, the building permit goes through the Town of Vail Community Development Department's Building Division, which inspects the ice barrier and underlayment before covering and the finished roof at final. Vail is about two and a half hours from Loveland by I-70 over Vail Pass, so we take on Vail work that justifies the mobilization: full replacements, multi-unit and HOA re-roofs, and custom homes. We stage materials on site, arrange crane lifts in the Village where there is no staging ground, keep the crew in the valley through dry-in, and work within the town's construction hour and ski-season limits. The season runs June through early October, and the DRB calendar adds weeks on the front end, so start with a free inspection in late winter.

faq.q: Does a re-roof in Vail need Design Review Board approval?
faq.a: Yes. Any exterior change, including a replacement roof, is reviewed against the town’s design standards, which list permitted and prohibited materials, require low-gloss metal with visual relief, and prohibit shedding snow onto entries, decks, and parking. We prepare the application with product data, color samples, and a snow retention drawing, and we attend the review if needed.

faq.q: What snow load does Vail require?
faq.a: The Town of Vail code sets a ground snow load of 142 pounds per square foot and roof snow loads of 100 psf below a 4:12 pitch and 80 psf at 4:12 and steeper. Decks and balconies carry the same loads. New roofs must also be designed so snow does not slide onto meters or neighboring property.

faq.q: Can I keep the cedar shake roof on my East Vail chalet?
faq.a: You can repair it once, for 25 percent or less of the roof area. Any larger repair or a second repair means replacing the entire covering with a Class A system, because wood shake is prohibited in Vail. Class A synthetic shake is the usual replacement when the look matters to you or your HOA.

faq.a: It is a two and a half hour drive, and we are honest about that. We take Vail projects that justify mobilizing a crew: full replacements, HOA and multi-unit re-roofs, and custom homes. We stage on site, keep the crew in the valley through dry-in, and manage the Design Review and HOA process so the distance never shows up in the schedule.

sections.h2: Cabins, lakes, and 8,245 feet of exposure

Red Feather Lakes is reached by a 24-mile county road west from US 287 at Livermore, and it feels every mile of it. The village sits at 8,245 feet among a dozen named lakes with a few hundred year-round residents and many more summer owners. The original 1920s cabins are still here, often hidden behind later additions, with low-pitched roofs, minimal overhangs, and whatever covering the last owner could haul up the hill. Around them are 1970s A-frames, 1990s and newer log and timber homes, and the Crystal Lakes and Glacier View subdivisions along the way in. The roofing we see most is aging asphalt shingle, old exposed-fastener metal, and the occasional cedar shake that should have come off twenty years ago.

At this elevation the sun is relentless and the wind off the Laramie River valley is steady. Hail does reach Red Feather Lakes from the storms that build over the Front Range foothills, though it is less frequent and usually smaller than what hits Fort Collins; a brittle, sun-aged shingle bruises from hail a new roof would shrug off, and we document that honestly on every inspection.

sections.h2: The Cameron Peak Fire and ember-resistant roofing
sections.html:
The Cameron Peak Fire started August 13, 2020, near Chambers Lake in the Roosevelt National Forest and grew into the largest wildfire in Colorado history at 208,663 acres before containment on December 2. Red Feather Lakes was under mandatory evacuation during the fire's eastward run in early September, and the fire destroyed 469 structures across its footprint, including more than 200 residences. The burn scar runs through the forest south and west of the village to this day.

The roof is where embers land. Replacing 25 percent or more of a roof covering triggers the full standard. We build every Red Feather roof to it. Standing seam metal is the usual answer on newer homes; Class A synthetic shake keeps the cabin look without the fuel. Our wildfire zone materials guide compares them.

sections.html: Larimer County sets ground snow loads by elevation, and at 8,000 feet the table reads 110 pounds per square foot, climbing fast above that. Many 1920s cabin rafters were never sized for that, so a heavier covering gets a structural look first. The county also requires Class 4 impact-rated asphalt shingles on any replacement roof, an ice barrier from the eave to at least two feet inside the exterior wall (metal panel roofs are exempt), metal valley flashing, drip edge, and a signed roofing certification stating the covering class and that manufacturer wind requirements were met. Much of the county is a high-wind area with design speeds of 140 miles per hour or more, and Red Feather's exposed ridges qualify. Repairs over 25 percent of the roof mean replacing the whole thing to current standards. For what that assembly looks like on a mountain cabin, read roofing a mountain home above 8,000 feet.

sections.h2: Permits, HOA covenants, and the drive from Loveland
sections.html:
Red Feather Lakes is unincorporated, so every re-roof permit goes through the Larimer County Building Division, which adopted the 2024 codes effective January 1, 2026. Roof repairs under one square are exempt; anything larger is permitted, and the inspector needs a secured ladder for any roof over 12 feet. Crystal Lakes, Glacier View, and several of the lake associations carry HOA covenants on roof color and material, and we prepare those submittals with product data and chips.

From Loveland the drive is about an hour and a quarter up US 287 and Red Feather Lakes Road, or longer by Highway 14 and County Road 68C through the Poudre Canyon. We schedule inspections and repairs in the same trip and stage full replacements with on-site delivery and a crew that stays through dry-in. The building season at 8,245 feet is late May through October. Start with a free photo-documented inspection, which is useful whether you live here year-round or only see the cabin in July.

faq.q: What does Larimer County require on a Red Feather Lakes re-roof?
faq.a: A Class A roof covering or assembly, Class 4 impact-rated shingles if asphalt is used, an ice barrier from the eave to two feet inside the exterior wall on non-metal roofs, metal valleys, drip edge, attachment rated for the site wind speed, and a signed roofing certification. Any repair over 25 percent of the roof means replacing the whole roof to these standards.

faq.q: Is my cabin in the Cameron Peak burn area subject to wildfire roofing rules?
faq.a: Larimer County already requires Class A roofs countywide, and the Red Feather Lakes Fire Protection District adopted the 2025 Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code in 2026, which adds ember-resistant vents, metal valleys over a cap sheet, and noncombustible gutters in mapped interface areas. We check the map for your parcel and build to the standard regardless.

faq.q: Can an old cabin roof carry a metal roof?
faq.a: Usually, because standing seam metal weighs less than the asphalt it replaces. The real question is whether the 1920s rafters carry the 110 pound per square foot ground snow load Larimer County assigns at 8,000 feet. We look at the framing during the inspection and tell you plainly if it needs reinforcement before any covering goes on.

faq.q: Does hail reach Red Feather Lakes?
faq.a: Yes, though less often and usually smaller than on the plains. Storms that build over the foothills push hail up the Livermore side, and a sun-aged shingle roof bruises easily. Class 4 impact-rated shingles are required by the county anyway, and metal handles the hail that reaches this elevation without trouble.

faq.q: How quickly can you get to Drake for a leak?
faq.a: Usually within a few days, because Drake is thirty minutes up US 34 from our Loveland office. We handle canyon repairs the same way we handle Loveland repairs: a photo-documented inspection, a written itemized estimate, and a repair crew that finishes and dries in the same day. US 34 closures for rockfall or construction are the only thing that slows us down.

faq.q: Does hail damage roofs in Drake?
faq.a: Yes, more than in the higher mountain towns. Drake is low enough in the canyon that storms building over the foothills push hail up US 34, usually smaller than Loveland sees but enough to bruise a sun-aged shingle roof. Larimer County requires Class 4 impact-rated shingles on replacement roofs for exactly this reason, and we document any hail marks we find.

faq.q: My cabin driveway crosses the river on a private bridge. Can you still deliver materials?
faq.a: Yes. We ask for the bridge weight rating up front and plan delivery around it, which may mean staging at the highway and ferrying bundles across in a lighter vehicle. We have done this on many Big Thompson Canyon properties and build the plan into the written estimate so the crew arrives knowing exactly how the site works.

faq.q: What roof is best for a Big Thompson Canyon home?
faq.a: Standing seam metal for longevity, snow shedding, ember resistance, and the canyon wind, or Class A synthetic shake where you want the cabin look. Both meet Larimer County’s Class A requirement and the Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code. If you stay with asphalt, the county requires Class 4 impact-rated shingles, which also handle the hail that reaches Drake.
